subtopic: EMPLOYMENT OF CHINESE ON STEAMSHIPS
EMPLOYMENT OF CHINESE ON STEAMSHIPS
speechtext:
The House having been informed on April 28th, 1924, that the Department of Immigration and Colonization had been asked and had given consent to the request of the British Empire Steel Corporation to be allowed to bring one hundred and five Chinese from England to be employed on certain boats of the company plying between the ports of Sydney, Louisburg, Halifax, St. John and Montreal, and that a bond had been deposited

Questions
by the company "which would be retained until the department is satisfied that all the Chinese covered by same have been checked out of Canada."
1.	If this consent was granted under the provisions of the Chinese Immigration Act of 1923, under what section is the authority to be found?
2.	If not under said act, under what other act and section can said authority be found?
3.	Prior to granting such consent had the attention of the department been directed to the provision of- (a) section 52 of the Immigration Act of 1910, being chapter 27 as re-enacted by subsection 3 of section 24 of the Immigration Act 1919, (b) section 1 of the Alien Labour Act, being chapter 97 of the Revised Statutes of 1906?

subtopic: EMPLOYMENT OF CHINESE ON STEAMSHIPS
speechtext:
1.	There is nothing in the Immigration Act and regulations or the Chinese Immigration Act of 1023. which strictly applies in a case of this kind. There are, however, precedents for the action taken by the Department of Immigration and Colonization. The practice of allowing Chinese to be brought forward for temporary employment on steamships during the summer months has been followed for a number of years past. In August, 1912, a Chinese crew of twenty-three was allowed to come forward for employment on the steamship Lingan. In August, 1914, a Chinese crew of thirty-three was brought out for the steamship Lingan. In December, 1915, four Chinese came forward for the same vessel. Again in August, 1916, thirty-three came out for the Lingan and thirty-two for the Hochelaga. Also in August, 1916, a Chinese crew of thirty-four was allowed to come forward for work on the steamship Rosecastle. In June, 1917, the Dominion Steel Corporation wrote the department that it was practically impossible to maintain native crews on their steamers, and one hundred and eight Chinese were brought from England for work on six of the company's coastal steamers. Also in June, 1917, twenty-seven Chinese were brought forward for the steamship Maskinonge. Again in February, 1923, seven Chinese came forward from England for employment on the steamship Kamaraska. In June, 1923, twenty were brought from England to man the steamship Rosecastle. In all of these cases a bond was furnished as a guarantee that the Chinese would be returned from Canada, at the conclusion of their employment, and the conditions of the bond were complied with. It must be remembered that in none of the cases referred to were these Chinese admitted to Canada within the meaning of the Immigration Act, but were simply allowed to come to Canada temporarily.

Resolution XIV of the Third Assembly of the League of Nations (1922) recommended for the consideration of the members of the league proposals made for a general treaty of mutual guarantee by the Temporary Mixed Commission. With regard to the adoption of a treaty

of mutual guarantee binding the parties to it to render assistance to a country which is attacked, the Canadian government represented lhat, the national conditions and geographical situation of the Dominion made it difficult for Canada to agree to such a treaty without much consideration and reservation. It was pointed out that the intention was that the obligation to render assistance should be limited in principle to those countries situated in the same part of the globe; that while Canada was situated in the North American continent, she Was a nation forming part of the British Empire and it therefore seemed difficult to devise a scheme which would give due effect to these conflicting considerations; it further seemed very unlikely that the Canadian people in the present circumstances would be prepared to consent to any agreement binding Canada to give assistance as proposed to other nations, and that therefore the government did not see its way to a participation in the treaty of mutual guarantee.
Following the 1923 Assembly of the League of Nations, a draft treaty of mutual assistance was also prepared by the Temporary Mixed Commission for the purpose of facilitating the reduction of armaments.contemplated by the covenant of the league. Certain confidential observations of the Imperial government, relative to the provisions of the draft treaty, have been communicated to the government of Canada, the most recent despatch thereon having been received by me since the question of the right hon. the leader of the opposition in the House yesterday. The provisions of [DOT]the draft treaty and observations thereon are at present under consideration by the government.

speechtext:
Hon. J. A. ROBB (Acting Minister of Finance) moved that the House go into committee of Supply:
Hon. GEORGE P. GRAHAM (Minister of Railways and Canals): Mr. Speaker, it is customary for the Minister of Railways to present the annual statement of the Canadian National Railways and the Canadian Merchant Marine before the Speaker leaves the chair.
I have laid on the Table, and hon. members will I think find copies in their post office boxes, the report of the Canadian National Railways, the report of the Vermont Central Railway, and the report of the Canadian Government Merchant Marine. Now, treating this question is rather dry work and I fear I shall have to ask the House to be patient with me; but I can assure hon. gentlemen that the reading of the statements which I shall submit is no more monotonous to them than it is to myself. Of necessity I have to read these statements, and again I ask the indulgence of the House if there seems to prevail a general monotony in these presentations. First of all I will take up the Canadian Government Merchant Marine.

The fifth annual report of the Canadian Government Merchant Marine, covering operations for the year 1923, is printed and is now being distributed. The gross revenues were $8,992,308 and the operating expenses, $10,856,601; entailing a deficit from operation of $1,864,293, compared with $2,384,189 in 1922. There was a decrease of $713,478 in gross revenue, a decrease of $1,233,374 in operating expenses and of $519,896 in the operating deficit. To the operating deficit is added accrued interest due the government, $4,495,184, and $3,008,192 for depreciation. These, with a reserve of $1,000 for doubtful debts and claims, bring the total loss for the year up to $9,368,670. The total deficit for the previous year was $9,649,478. The improvement therefore was $280,808.
Sir Henry Thornton's report is as follows:
The main reasons for the decrease in operating deficit were the cancellation of South American, Mediterranean and certain other unremunerative services, also the curtailment as far as possible of general expenses.
As a result of the strikes which occurred at Cardiff, Swansea, London, Antwerp and Vancouver, sailings were considerably interfered with and gross receipts and net earnings were in each case diminished.
Generally speaking full cargoes on outward trips were secured, but satisfactory cargoes were not obtainable for homeward trips, which naturally increased operating expenses out of all proportion to operating revenues.
During the year different vessels were chartered for carriage of grain on the Great Lakes and for carriage of pulpwood in the St. Lawrence Gulf trade.
Fleet-The fleet consists of sixty vessels, particulars of which are attached. The remaining four vessels previously included in the fleet, namely the " Canadian Settler," " Thos. J. Drummond," " J. A. McKee " and the "Sheba," were sold at satisfactory prices. Offers received for certain others were not sufficiently attractive to make acceptance advisable.
Insurance-Since April 1, 1923, insurance was provided out of the company's own insurance fund, the result being a credit balance of approximately $318,795.47, all of which is invested in Dominion of Canada bonds.
The vessels whether in active service or not have been kept in a high state of efficiency and repair.
No total losses occurred during the year and the number of minor accidents was small.
Trade Routes-In November, 1923, a new monthly service was inaugurated between Vancouver and the United Kingdom. It is expected that this will provide accommodation for farmers in the western provinces and shippers and exporters on the Pacific coast.
Eight of the smaller vessels have been utilized in the grain trade on the Great Lakes. Four of the vessels trading to United Kingdom ports were fitted in the spring for the carriage of cattle. During the St. Lawrence navigation season several of the smaller vessels were used in the carriage of pulpwood from the Maritime provinces to Quebec and Ontario points.
Recommendations-It is still the feeling of the directors that the recommendations made last year in regard to reduction of capital cost of the fleet and to the interest payable to the government should be carried out.
Management-The directors wish to record their appreciation of the satisfactory services rendered by the officers, employees and crews in the company's service during the year.
Does the minister inelude interest charges in the operating costs?
We include a depreciation of $3,000,000.

And $4,000,-
000 in interest.

Yes, but that is noted in the deficit; it is not included in the operating costs. In calculating the deficit, the sum of $4,000,000 due the government in interest is taken into account. I come now to the Canadian National Railways.

I am now in a position to bring down the detailed report on operations of the Canadian National System for 1923 which the Chairman and President of the Board of Directors, Sir Henry Thornton, has placed in my hands for presentation to parliament. Hon. gentlemen will appreciate that the first year's operation of the combined and consolidated system has been conducted under difficulties due to changes in management,

C.N.R.-Minister's Statement
in location, in personnel and in administrative methods. The present management did not become wholly effective until May 1st, 1923, with the selection of Montreal as headquarters and the division of the immense territory covered by the system into separate regions for convenience of local administration and operation. This involved change of residence for the majority of the administrative and operative staffs, and the transfer and disturbance of records. All this tended to unsettlement, notwithstanding which the management has been able to build up a most effective operating machine, with an absence of friction and an esprit de corps that has resulted in an improvement of service that has been freely acknowledged by the patrons of the National lines.
While new methods have been required to cope with conditions involved by coordinated and consolidated management and operation, it has not, for various reasons, been possible to abandon corporate accounting and record. This also has tended to make difficult the earlier production of complete and detailed figures. However, I am now in a position to read to the House Sir Henry Thornton's first annual report of his stewardship, and that of his co-directors. It has been certified by the firm of auditors who conduct continuous audit of the books and accounts of the National System, and is in printed form, together with statistical detail. And when I lay the report on the Table of the House, before I sit down-as a matter of fact I have done this-copies of the report, with that of the Central Vermont separately printed, will be in the hands of the postal officials of the House and Senate for immediate distribution.
The report, which is dated May 1st, gives the steam operated mileage as 21,851 and divides it not only into regions but into mileage owned, mileage operated under lease or contract and mileage operated under trackage rights. Incidentally I may say that the report is accompanied by a very useful map which outlines the various operating regions in different colours.
Revenue and Expenses
The operating revenue for 1923 was $254,926,456, as compared with $234,059,025, in 1922 an increase of $20,867,431. The revenue is split into that derived from freight, from passenger, from mail and from miscellaneous services. All of these show increases with the exception of revenue from mails.
The working expenses for 1923 were $234,689,892, compared with $231,172,313, the previous year, an increase of $3,517,579. The

working expenses are also split to show the customary detail, and the net earnings were $20,236,563, in contrast with $2,886,711 in 1922, an increase of $17,349,851.54. The operating ratio was 92.06.
The foregoing is a summary of a full page of figures. I will now proceed to read Sir Henry Thornton's report:
Canadian National Railways-Sir Henry Thornton's Report
Gross Earnings
The increase in revenues is particularly gratifying, and speaks for itself. An excellent crop contributed materially to this satisfactory showing. The fundamental necessity	of the system is to	build	up its	grossearnings to such	a figure as will be	consistent in	somedegree with its large mileage, and every effort is being addressed to this objective. Freight and passenger traffic returns for the year both show a material improvement over the previous year. With the single exception of September, when the grain movement was somewhat retarded, each month's gross revenue has shown a satisfactory increase over the corresponding month of 1922. The financial performance of the system will turn very largely upon the constantly increasing gross	receipts, and the	board	notes	withsatisfaction the	zeal and energy	which the traffic
department and all in the service of the company have displayed in this direction.
Operating Expenses
A comparison of operating expenses shows that there was a reduction of $841,760 in expenses chargeable to maintenance of way and structures, and of $3,984,380 in those attributable to maintenance of equipment.
With respect to maintenance of way and structures, the saving was largely the result of the performance of work during that season of the year when its accomplishment involved a minimum cost both from the point of view of price of labour and interruptions from traffic. Considerable attention was also given to improvement of work and the maintenance of certain sections of the system at a standard consistent with the character of the traffic. Notwithstanding a reduction in maintenance of way and structures expenses, the general standard of the roadbed has not only been maintained, but an improvement has been accomplished.
The reduction in expenses chargeable to maintenance of equipment is largely due to the fact that in the year 1922 a deferred maintenance of equipment reserve was created by charges amounting to $4,490,000 whereas in 1923 charges under this heading amounted to $801,402. The difference in these charges in 1923 as compared with 1922, amounted to $3,688,598. All deferred maintenance of equipment charges, may now be considered as either having been overtaken or provided for in the above-mentioned reserve. The balance of the saving in maintenance of equipment expenses may be attributed to more economical working.

Will the hon. gentleman permit a question there? Other members may understand the matter, but I do not. What is really the significance of the last two sentences about the change of the reserve from 1922 explaining the change in the equipment expenses?

There was, as I understand it, an equipment fund to catch up to what is termed deferred maintenance, that

C.N.R.-Minister's Statement
is, maintenance that should have been paid for in the years before. This amount of $4,000,000 was set up as a reserve out of which to pay the deferred maintenance. As far as I understand it that is the explanation.
For the twelve months ended December 31, 1923, the average number of freight cars awaiting repairs represented 6.2 per cent of the total freight car equipment, as compared with an average of 8.2 per cent for what are termed " Class 1 " railways in the United States. With respect to locomotives awaiting repairs on the Canadian National Railways, the average figure for 1923 was 22.88 per cent, while for " Class 1 " American railways it was 21.35 per cent. From this it will be seen that the general condition of equipment on the Canadian National Railways was comparable with the better class railways across the border, and it is a reasonable deduction that expenses chargeable to maintenance of equipment are ample.
Transportation Expenses
Transportation expenses increased by $6,654,475 and absorbed 47.18 per cent of the gross earnings, as compared with 48.57 per cent in 1922, in the face of an increase in the gross earnings of $20,867,430. That is to say, gross earnings increased 8.9 per cent and expenses chargeable to moving the * traffic increased 5.8 per cent. While these figures are indicative of a healthy improvement, a fruitful field for* further reductions exists which will be cultivated with energy throughout the year 1924.
Transportation expenses vary with gross earnings, and the larger the volume of business the greater is the amount consumed in its movement. While such increases are inevitable the objective to be sought is a minimum increase in transportation expenses as gross receipts increase.
In the consideration of transportation expenses efficiency of organization plays a large part and it is fair to point out that the present transportation organization did not begin to function as an entity in all of its details until the latter part of the year. This is abundantly demonstrated by the fact that in the latter months of 1923 and the early months of 1924 the percentage of gross earnings absorbed by transportation expenses represented a constantly decreasing figure. It is not unreasonable to assume that these expenses in 1924 will show material improvement.
Traffic Expenses
Traffic expenses increased by $537,681. This was largely due to a more aggressive policy in the solicitation of business, advertising, and similar items. In view of the large increase in gross earnings, the increase in expenses chargeable to traffic is modest; indeed it is believed that a further increase in such expenses would be productive of a larger gross revenue. It is the intention of the administration actively to pursue this policy and, where an adequate return is assured, unhesitatingly to assume expense.
Prior to the consolidation certain expenditures required for developing traffic were postponed. These expenditures as well as those in connection with the new Colonization and Development Department were undertaken during the year and partly account for the increase in traffic expenses.
General Expenses
General expenses increased by $814,966. A large proportion of this was due to reorganization, the preparation and establishment of new offices, the moving of officers and employees to their new headquarters, much of which would naturally be expected
in the adjustment of the new organization and will not be recurrent. Increases in law expenses, including litigation costs, and pensions accounted for about half of the increase in general expenses.
Income Items
In an examination of the income statement, a decrease of $2,170,286 will be observed in total nonoperating income.
In 1922 substantial profits were made in exchange on purchase of sterling funds. In 1923 the profit was less by $1,000,000. In order to comply with the requirements of the Interstate Commerce Commission in connection with a settlement with the United States government for the guarantee period 1920 a debit of $1,457,562 was made against income account, with no corresponding entry for 1922. These two amounts were the main items producing the above decrease.
Might I point out here that when the United States government gave certain guarantees to the railways of the United States through what is known as the guarantee period, each railway was asked to present an account. I am told that the Grank Trunk and the Grand Trunk Western lines, in common with all the other lines in the United States, had not time to make out with any great accuracy a detailed report in 1920, but they put in their accounts an amount which they thought would cover what was due them under this guarantee. This year when the final accounts were adjusted it was discovered that the railways in the United States belonging to the Canadian National had an account that was top-heavy by $1,457,000. So that sum was charged against the income of the railway for 1923, although it is not really a proper charge for that account, but it had to be adjusted.

Had the
larger item been taken into income before, although not paid?
I think so.

Is my hon.
friend clear about that? Of course, it would be quite improper to make the entry in this way unless that had been done.
I am told that the larger amount had been carried forward in the books of the company.

That is very
different from bringing it into income receipts.

But it brings about the
same net result whether it comes in by one door or 'the other.

In one case it
comes in, in the other it stays out.

C.N.R.-Minister's Statement

The railway had to debit this item of $1,457,000 against income account in connection with the readjustment with the United States government.
Perhaps it would not be out of place to mention light here another item which this year is paid by the railway or charged up to it, but which never came to the accounts before, namely, an item in connection with Grand Trunk Pacific interest. It will be remembered that under the contract with the Grand Trunk Pacific that road was relieved from the payment of interest in. respect of the mountain section for seven years, without recourse. The seven years have expired and this year that interest, amounting to $1,600,000, is charged up to the Canadian National Railways. If these two items of the expense charged this year to the Canadian National, and never heretofore charged, are deducted, a betterment will be shown of $3,000,000 in the Canadian National budget. After accounting for fixed charges and all increases the amount instead of being something over $6,000,000 is, with these two items considered, something over $9,000,000.

May I get that clear?
Do I understand the minister to say that the Grand Trunk in respect of its contingent guarantee of Grand Trunk Pacific bond interest-
No, that is not it.
Then I have not got it at all.

I will get it right: For the first seven years the interest was payable by the government, under the contract. That seven years has expired. Now the interest is payable by the Canadian National Railways having taken over the Grand Trunk Pacific.
Did they pay it?
It is charged up in their debit account-
But not paid.

It is not paid, but it is charged up against the Canadian National Railways. This is the first year it has been so charged, but I may say, to be fair, that it will have to be charged against the Canadian National Railways every year hereafter.
And saved to the government.

The government paid it during the last seven years, but the government will not hereafter have to pay it, except as they meet deficits of the Canadian National Railways.
Hire of Freight Cars-Debit Balance
The assembling of cars for the western crop movement, and the inevitable delay resulting to coal cars used in accumulating a large reserve of fuel (which indications of a miners' strike made a proper precaution) necessarily resulted in a large increase in the amount paid to other carriers for use of cars. The results obtained, however, amply justified this course of action and the expenditure involved. Available car supply through this means was increased by 7.6 per cent. The service obtained per car per day was increased by 5.6 per cent, permitting additional freight tonnage to be handled, which, notwithstanding the lower average of freight rates, produced increased freight earnings of $15,457,000.
It is expected that still greater efficiency in car service will be obtained during the coming year, but this will not prevent a further increase in adverse per diem balance if revenue traffic continues to increase.
Balance Sheet
A consolidated balance sheet has been prepared which includes the capital accounts of the railways and subsidiary companies comprising the national system.
There are securities in the hands of the public of a total par value of $823,099,056. In addition to this, there is an amount expended by the government to construct and equip the Intercolonial and the Transcontinental, and to purchase various branches in the province of Quebec and in the Maritime provinces which form the old Canadian Government Railways, the capital investment and operations of which are duly set forth in the system consolidated balance sheet.
To those hon. members who possibly have mot had an opportunity of studying that question I may say that on the expenditure on government railways there has never been any interest charged.
As shown in the income statement, fixed charges for the year total $65,199,323, being an increase of $5,798,847 over 1922, practically all of which was on account of interest charged by the government. Of the total fixed charges mentioned above, $35,041,380 was paid to the public.
To make that clear, let me interpolate this: While the government has advanced many millions to the Canadian National. Railways, that interest is all taken into account, together with the interest due to the public, and it has been thought by some that the statement presented to the House from time to time by different governments included only the interest due the public and not the interest due the government. The statement as charged against t'he Canadian National Railways includes all the interest payable to the government and payable to the public as well.
Consideration is being given to the policy to be followed with respect to the capitalization of the system, and the extent to which, if at all, the advances

C.N.R.-Minister's Statement
made and capital held by the government should be written down to a figure which may be regarded as consistent with the earning prospects of the railway. In the consideration of such a problem, the interests of the government, which is to say the people of Canada, must be given due weight. On the other hand it would seem unreasonable to burden the Canadian National Railways with a load which is beyond its conceivable earning capacity. The directors have this problem under consideration but before any definite recommendations can be made, a careful survey must be made of the capital position of the company, not only with a view to meeting the difficulty explained in this paragraph but also to simplifying and consolidating a variety of securities outstanding.

Finance
Of the $74,550,000 voted by parliament for the fiscal year ended March 31st, 1924, there was advanced in cash by the government to the company $24,550,000, the balance being represented by the $50,000,000 of thirty-year 5 per cent guaranteed bonds issued in February, 1924. As of August 1st last an issue was made of $22,500,000 of the company's fifteen-year 5 per cent bonds guaranteed by the Dominion government, but additionally secured by $30,000,000 worth of equipment in connection with which the bonds were issued.
Are all the liabilities in now?
Each year the liabilities must increase, in one way, as against the increased earnings, as money is borrowed year by year either from the government or from the public.
That will be new money.
That will be new money, and an additional liability.
And additional assets, too.

this unit of earning up to a point approximately 75 per cent over the pre-war level. The series of reductions which began January 1, 1921, have substantially reduced this average so that in 1923 it stood at 0.980 or 32 per cent above the pre-war level. In contrast to this the average prices of labour, material and supplies prevailing in 1923 were somewhat in excess of 90 per cent over the pre-war scale.
The Canadian National railway system is the property of the people of Canada, and it is for the people, through their duly elected parliamentary representatives and the Board of Railway Commissioners, to determine what the freight and passenger rate policy of the Dominion in its relation to the Canadian National railway system shall be; but there is no way by which freight and passenger rates can be continually reduced and net earnings at the same time increased; and, moreover, restricted net earnings must inevitably mean additional taxes to provide for annual deficits. The administration of the Canadian National railways system is the trustee of the people's property. That administration cannot and has no desire to dictate policies, but it would be lacking in the [DOT]fulfilment of its public duties if it did not make these facts clear to the people of Canada.
Betterments
During the year important progress was made on the general improvement programme which has been carried on during the period of government control. The expenditures have been large, but have not been out of proportion to the corresponding expenditures made by other large systems on this continent, and the improved operating results could not have been obtained without such expenditures and the acquisition of additional rolling stock and motive power. The properties of the system have been brought up to a standard which will enable the handling of increased traffic in the future with normal expenditures, except so far as affected by new business developments.
To obtain proper results from operating as a single system lines which previously were in competition, it was necessary to build a number of connecting lines and cut-offs, the construction of which has permitted short and economical routing of traffic, joint use of terminals, stations, offices and other facilities with consequent reduction in operating expense, increased capacity for handling the volume of business and ability to give improved service to the public. During the period of improvement, various grade reductions have 'been undertaken; water supply, particularly in western 'Canada, has been greatly improved; terminals have been enlarged and modernized; some sections of the rrailway have been double-tracked; signals have been installed; a great many tie plates have been applied; heavier rails have been laid; bridges, trestles and [DOT]culverts have been strengthened, renewed or replaced *with permanent work; tie renewals have been brought up to a proper basis and a start has been made on the use of treated ties. Much ballasting has been undertaken, although much remains to be done. A number of station buildings have been constructed; some enlarged or replaced. Telegraph and telephone communications have been bettered.
In addition to the cars purchased, there were a number rebuilt, reinforced and in other ways improved. Various items of special equipment were applied to locomotives such as feed water heaters, automatic stokers, boosters, superheaters, etc., and a number of locomotives were converted or rebuilt. The gradual use of heavier power over the various lines as their physical condition permits, and as traffic is developed, tends more and more to efficient operation.
Land Sales
Conditions in the farming industry in western Canada are not yet such as encourage the ready sale of lands.

61,994 acres were sold in 1923 at an average price of $15.66 per acre, amounting to $970,952.	9,025 acres were
sold in 1922 at an average price of $16.67 per acre, amounting to $150,531.14.
When cancellations of purchase contracts are considered, the showing is still more favourable. In 1923 the cancellations represented 59,190 acres as against 114,056 acres in 1922. Fewer cancellations are expected in 1924.
Wages and Labour
Various demands were made by employees during the year for increases in wages and improvements in working conditions. Several requests for increases are under consideration at the present time. There was no loss of time by reason of strikes among the railways' employees during the year. General good feeling prevails in all classes.
The total expenditure for labour during the year chargeable to operating expenses was $136,463,470 representing 58.15 per cent of such expenses, as compared with 54.99 per cent in 1922.
Purchases and Stores
All purchases for the Canadian National Railways and subsidiaries, including the Canadian Government Merchant Marine, are under the jurisdiction of the Purchasing Department, with headquarters in Montreal. There are purchasing agents located in the various regions to handle local buying. In the work of the department is included the custody and distribution of stores and materials. The reclamation of material and the sale of scrap, through which very substantial savings are effected, also comes under the Purchasing and Stores Department.
Express
This service is now carried on by the railway company itself instead of by the express company. Economies and other advantages have resulted from the change. The gross express receipts and the expenses of the express department are included in the system's revenue and expense accounts, whereas, generally speaking, other railways show only the net earnings earned by transporting express matter.
The operations of the express department present a large and fruitful field which merits a progressive and aggressive policy. It is the intention of the Company during the coming year to expand the activities of the express department into foreign fields, not only with the view of securing a large volume of traffic, but also in the provision of travellers' cheques and various other financial arrangements necessary to the comfort and welfare of tourists.
Telegraphs
The Canadian National Telegraphs operate commercial telegraph lines throughout the Dominion west of Moncton, N.B., and have charge of the maintenance of all telegraph and telephone lines used for railway purposes.
Material improvement has been made in the efficiency of the telegraph department during the year. Better and more satisfactory offices have been provided at several places, the messenger service has been smartened and every effort is being made to provide a standard of service which will excite a greater business.
Insurance
The Insurance Department was reorganized in March, 1923, and placed under the control of a Director of Insurance. At the same time the Company decided to extend over the whole system the principle of selfinsurance which had previously been in effect to a limited extent on parts of the system. The wisdom of this policy has been amply justified, as although there was paid into the fund approximately $250,000 less than had previously been paid to underwriters, a surplus of $1,014,014 was accumulated from April 1st to December 31st.

C.N.R.-Minister's Statement
This surplus together with the previous surplus amounted in the aggregate as of December 31st, 1923, to $3,133,735, practically all of which is invested in Dominion Government securities. The intention is to build up this fund as rapidly as possible.
An entirely new recording system has been devised, which results in a determination of the exact status of the insurance fund with respect to premiums and losses on the various classes of risks insured therein.
A fire prevention and inspection staff has been organized under the direction of a competent fire prevention engineer, and is concentrating its efforts towards a reduction in losses. Various other steps have been taken to reduce fire losses, and it is anticipated that within the next year the system will have a fire insurance, prevention and inspection system second to none.
Colonization and Development
During the past year the matter of immigration has been receiving very close attention in governmental and railway circles. Its success depends first, upon the choico of suitable immigrants; secondly, upon the suitable location of such immigrants; and, thirdly, upon the supervision and assistance of them till they become self-supporting. Having this in view it was decided to open in London, England, a special office under the jurisdiction of the Department of Colonization and Development. Dr. W. J. Black who, after many years of special experience in agriculture and immigration, held the position of Deputy Minister of Immigration at Ottawa, has been appointed European manager of such office. Prior to his leaving for England recently, special meetings were held in Montreal at which there were present representatives of the Dominion government, the national railways and allied steamship companies-the desire being to determine a policy of which all interested parties would approve, and which would be carried out in a spirit of co-operation.
The present work of colonization and development of natural resources is being carried on from centres such as Montreal, Winnipeg, Edmonton, London, England, and Paris, France, with branches at St. Paul, Seattle and Boston in the United States.
Was the Canadian Pacific in that?

It does not say so in
the present report, but the Canadian Pacific is engaged in exactly similar work, and I think there is a good deal of co-operation between the Canadian Pacific railway and the government lines.
It embraces advertising of lands and business opportunities, the distribution of information in the public press and by lectures, folders, pamphlets, maps, etc., the answering of inquiries, etc., advising and assisting incoming settlers in regard to choice of lands and the obtaining of employment. The work in the New England States has resulted in the repatriation of French Canadians in western Canada, Quebec and northern Ontario. Up to the present time satisfactory results have been produced in spite of the recent agricultural depression, but the more important part of the work done during the past year was the establishment of a suitable organization which will be able to assist in completing the work expected to result from the intensive immigration policy now being carried on and which includes the group settlement arrangements made with the Overseas Settlement Board.
The following represents the broad principles upon which it is intended to carry on with vigour the colonization work of the Canadian National Railway System.
1.	To influence the immigration and satisfactory settlement in Canada of the largest possible number of people of productive capacity which the country can absorb and assimilate;
2.	To contribute to the dissemination of information concerning the vast and extensive natural resources of the Dominion and the widespread opportunities for industrial development, so that capital may be attracted from other countries and invested where enterprise will be legitimately rewarded;
3.	To promote the land settlement of new Canadians under conditions that will ensure the maximum success in their farming operations and enable them to enjoy such social and religious institutions as are necessary to individual happiness and contentment;

Radio Department
A Radio department was organized during the latter part of 1923 under the control of a radio engineer and an assistant. The work undertaken during the year was largely experimental, and principally in connection with the operation of radio on moving trains. Various tests having been made and excellent results obtained, wireless receiving instruments are now being installed upon the principal transcontinental trains, and similar sets are being placed in a number of the company's hotels. It is the intention, in the introduction of radio telephony on the lines of the Canadian National railways, to provide a ready means of communication between the executive officers of the railway and the public, to advertise Canada and the Canadian National railways, to furnish entertainment to

C.N.R.-Minister's Statement
passengers on long distance trains and guests at the company's hotels, and generally to make the service of the railway more attractive to the travelling and shipping public. But more important still is the desire to establish that human contact between the officers of the company and the employees which it is considered is essential to the maintenance of loyalty and efficiency. The company has arranged for wireless receiving sets to be procured by its employees at a reasonable price and on easy terms. Considerable advantage has already been taken of this, and in the course of a comparatively short time it is hoped that it will be possible for the executive officers of the company to address personally a large proportion of the employees in their own homes. As an advertising medium radio telephony is unsurpassed, and the administration believes that in the establishment of a radio department it has taken a unique and constructive step in railway operation.
Organization
When the present Board of Directors took charge of the property represented by the Canadian National Railway system, two separate organizations existed, namely the Grand Trunk Railway and the Canadian National Railways of that day. Within the limitations imposed by conditions much co-ordination had already been accomplished and many improvements and economies introduced. The administrative work performed by these two organizations laid the foundation for what was to follow, and the present Board desires to record its recognition of the valuable work performed by the boards of directors and officers of the previous organizations.
The task, however, of determining the organization best suited for the administration of so large a property, extending from the Atlantic to the Pacific and including telegraph and express companies, as well as a Merchant Marine, can only be characterized as formidable. All of the great railway systems of North America and Europe have been the result of decades of growth and development in which ample time was afforded for the development of an organization and the education and trial of those who have subsequently become trusted and capable officers. To a large degree the Board of Directors was obliged to evolve within a few months a consolidated organization appropriate to the needs of the widely-flung system committed to its charge. Officers were obliged to acquaint themselves not' only with the new territories, but with each other. New channels for the flow of reports and instructions had to be provided, a system of statistical information developed which would readily reveal the operating results of the various departments and the danger points to be guarded against and many other important details which will at once be apparent to those familiar with the organization of a large undertaking. It would be remarkable if the accomplishment of such a task were unaccompanied by mistakes; but if such mistakes have been made they have been of relatively small importance, and have not materially affected the general result for the year. No doubt as months go by errors will be detected and improvements made.
Perhaps the most gratifying feature of the year's operations has been the development of a fine spirit of loyalty, co-operation and pride in the undertaking amongst officers and employees alike. Much of the satisfactory financial performance has been due to this spirit. Those employees and officers of the company who come in contcat with the travelling and shipping public have assisted greatly in establishing an excellent feeling by their courtesy and attention to the patrons of the system. The principle that the passenger is always to be regarded as the guest of the company has been splendidly maintained by all.

The board has much pleasure in congratulating all in the employ of the company upon the efficiency of their efforts, and cordially thanks them for their loyal support.
While business and industrial conditions in their relation to and effect upon the national railway system in all sections of the Dominion have received thoughtful and sympathetic consideration, the position in the Maritime provinces seems to call for special comment.
In those provinces there appears to exist a feeling of disappointment and dissatisfaction in a way, which is not clearly revealed, that the provinces have not obtained that advantage from Confederation which they had been led to expect. The consideration of such a problem is obviously beyond the scope and responsibilities of the administration of the national railway system, but when dissatisfaction in any section of the Dominion reaches such proportions as to involve a possible effect upon the company's operations, it is desirable that at least some attention should be given and it is for this reason that the subject is mentioned in this report.
With a view to improving the position in the Maritime provinces, the efforts of the traffic department of the railway have been addressed in various directions, and as a result the sailings from the port of Halifax have been increased from 491 in 1922 to 768 in 1923. The Canadian National Railways recognize the importance of the ports of St. John and Halifax, and the useful part they should both play in the development of Canadian marine traffic. Nothing within reason will be left undone to promote increased business through these gateways. For some time there had been a differential of one cent per hundred pounds against the port of Halifax on export and import freight and this has been removed, Halifax being now on the same basis as all other Atlantic ports served by the Canadian National Railways. In addition to the removal of this differential, tariffs covering certain contemplated reductions of class rates are now in the course of preparation. These reductions in some cases will run as high as 15 per cent. During the past twelve months a revision of freight rates to and from Prince Edward Island has been completed, placing them on the same basis as is applicable to the mainland, while formerly a somewhat higher scale was applied. Certain other minor reductions in other freights were also made.
These matters are mentioned in order that it may be understood that the Canadian National Railways are, within the limits of their ability, endeavouring to do everything possible to better transportation conditions in the Maritime provinces. The recent visit to the Eastern provinces of a number of members of parliament from western Canada will, it is hoped, have a good effect in enabling the people from the extreme parts of Canada to become better acquainted with the difficulties which confront both eastern and western Canada.
The business done through the Canadian Atlantic ports is capable of much greater expansion, in the accomplishment of which expansion mutual under, standing between the eastern, western and central portions of Canada is essential. Several suggestions have been made to the Canadian National Railways management as to how this desired result might best be brought about, but as the province of the management of the railway system is to deal solely with transportation this large question of policy must be left to the government and to parliament.

Capital Expenditures Justify Themselves
Sir Henry Thornton makes it clear that restriction of maintenance had no part in the improved results obtained in the year under review. The amount of money required to put the Canadian National system in good shape has been large, but not unduly so when the mileage involved is taken into account. But for these capital expenditures on road and equipment the improved performance now in evidence would not have been possible. The money which is spent last on a railway is held to be the most profitable investment on account of the definite knowledge then available as to where to spend it, and the operating officials of the Canadian National Railways feel that without the capital expenditures of the last five years the National system, as at present constituted, would not have paid operating expenses this year. Lacking these vital expenditures the system would be entirely inadequate, with transportation facilities limited, and in no position to play a proper part in the development of the country.

Before concluding I want to make an appeal to the House. As I said before, parliament desires only to make a success of this great enterprise. That can only be done by the cooperation of parliament; it can only be done by the sympathetic co-operation of parliament. This is the business of all the people of Canada, and we, representing them, hope to continue to carry it on in a way that will merit the confidence of parliament. A few weeks ago my good friend Mr. Beatty of the' Canadian Pacific Railway Company, speaking at their annual meeting, referred to a disadvantage under which his private company operated in Canada and mentioned in that connection a certain section of the Canadian National Railway Act. That section provides that the location of lines shall be subject to the Minister of Railways, while in the case of the Canadian Pacific the location of lines is subject to the Board of Railway Commissioners. Mr. Beatty complained that that was an advantage to the Canadian National and consequently a disadvantage to the Canadian Pacific. I might name another advantage which perhaps the Canadian National has and to which reference was made a few moments ago, namely that the people of Canada and the resources of Canada are behind it in the guarantee of its securities. I do not know why that section was put in the Canadian National Railway Act. I suppose those who framed it must have had some good reason for putting it in. But granted there is a disadvantage, I submit that under present conditions the disadvantage of a private company in Canada in these two respects could be multiplied by one hundred and then would not be comparable with the disadvantage under which the Canadian National Railways operate.
Let me put this to you-I am talking very frankly: Suppose Mr. Beatty's shareholders met and stayed in session four or five months every year; suppose every day a portion of his staff was compelled to be taken from their work to answer all kinds of questions; suppose that Mr. Beatty-I mean the president of any private company-were accused of all kinds of things; suppose that among his shareholders there was a large number who made no bones about declaring him and his board of management incompetent; what would Mr. MAY 28, 1924
C.N.R.-Minister's Statement
Beatty do? He would resign in five minutes. He could not operate without the confidence of his directors, through his shareholders.
Suppose, in addition, that Mr. Beatty was compelled to answer a question like this: Why was John Smith put off the road as gatekeeper in such and such a township? Who bought the uniforms for officials and employees of the Canadian Pacific Railway? Prom whom were they bought, how much was paid for them and who got them? I am not trying to indulge in ridicule, but I am tiying to point out the situation. I want to make it clear that under the present system of government, every member of this House has the technical right to ask all these questions, and more too. Do not misunderstand me. Every member of this House has the right to know where every dollar goes, who gets it, and what he gets it for, no matter what the detail is; that is his technical right. But I appeal to the members of the House if the Canadian National Railways can be run successfully if those rights are exercised to the limit?
I am anxious, as the mouthpiece of the Canadian National Railways, to give all the information possible, but I appeal to members that if we are going to make a success of this great enterprise, we must allow it to function approximately under the same conditions as a private company. Parliament itself has changed the conditions in this coum-try. Not the government, but the people of Canada through parliament have entered upon a gigantic scale of railway operation. Now if they wish to make a success of this enterprise upon which they have engaged, I appeal again to the members of the House to think seriously whether they should not forego what is their technical right of asking for information that never would be given to a shareholder, and much of which would never be
given to a director. I am a shareholder of some companies, and I am a director of some, or have been, and I know that when the directors meet, the shares are represented by the men sitting around the table nine times out of ten, and very often no information except what is printed is given to any shareholder. I do not say that is right, but I do say that when the Parliament of Canada has passed an act establishing a company to operate their property, and it is the greatest railway transportation property in the world, they should give it approximately the same rights as are given by the shareholders of a private company in which they have put their own money.
I believe that this system can be made a success. I believe that with careful operation, with close scrutiny, and with business acumen, in a very few years the Canadian National Railways will be able to meet its obligations to the public. When that is done, a great step has been taken, and after that, if it be possible, its obligations to the government can be gradually recognized.
I do not think, Mr. Speaker, I can say anything more, but I appeal to the members of the House, in dealing with their own property, to give the men they have engaged to manage the property a square deal, and a deal comparable to that whicT, would be given to them by shareholders who had put up the money out of their own pockets into a private company.
I wish to ask the privilege of the House to put on Hansard, without reading it, this statement respecting the Canadian National Railways, including the Central Vermont Railway.

(Leader of the Opposition):	Mr. Speaker, my first
suggestion to the minister would be that in respect of the annual railway statement it would probably be an improvement if the reports of the president were treated similarly to the statement to which he has just referred, and included in Hansard without perusal. I say that, not in any spirit of cynicism or sarcasm towards the report. It must have impressed all hon. members, though, that the report was extremely long in detail; I will not say confused; but because of the necessity of being cumbered with so much of technical and financial language it was not easily absorbed by hon. members by a mere listening in the House. The reading of it had the effect of burying the minister's latter presentation under a deluge of technical railway terminology, so much so that many hon. members escaped, and those who were here I fear scarcely understood even the clear presentation he made at the last.
I urged a year ago that we should, in the matter of our railway reports to parliament, observe as far as possible a sequence in the whole system and order of presentation. If we do not, we are never going to be able to really grasp and understand the subject. I cannot see very much of the parallel in the method the minister adopts this year with that he adopted a year ago, and had I not previously been armed with at least some experience with this question, and particularly with some facts which the minister gave me himself, I am afraid I would have come away very little enlightened by what I have listened to this afternoon.
May I make a reference to the minister's last appeal before I go farther? I am one of those who, I think, can be counted a friend of the National Railways; I would be a very strange individual if I were not. I am one of those, I think one of millions, one of the vast majority of the people of Canada, the almost unanimous total of the people of Canada, who wish earnestly and hopefully success to this system. Nor would I be a party to any course of conduct which sought to imperil that success. I am one of those who believe as well that we have launched the right machinery by which we can best of all hope to make a success of this great enterprise. Canada is in a position unique in the world. With less than nine millions of people, we have the largest single railway enterprise in the world, our possession and our responsibility. No nation five times our size, or ten times, no nation however large, has a parallel responsibility at all. In so far then as the duty of managing a great business venture goes, Canada 
stands in a place by herself in the world. The first great difficulty was to plan a scheme by which there could be a prospect of making it go. The incorporation of a company with the stock owned by the nation and the appointment of a directorate corresponding to the directorate of a private company was the plan suggested and approved. We now have had some years of experience. While these years have not been fruitful of what could be called unmixed success, nevertheless they have at least taught us this lesson that no better scheme could have been launched and that there was no better system of machinery by which we could have hoped to attain success earlier or more abundant.
We now also have the precept of another body of men who were shouldered with tremendous responsibility too and were asked to devise for the management of a corresponding venture in the Old Land, a system or a mechanism, and who have reported in favour of just such a one as has already been tried in Canada. I refer to the Dawes Reparation Commission, dealing with the question of German reconstruction. They recommend for the management of the railway system of Germany, already for many years the property of the state, a change, placing that management on the corporate basis and under a directorate exactly the same or virtually the same as we have had in this Dominion. So we started right.
There were dangers ahead, as everybody understood. Some of the dangers the Ministei of Railways has alluded to in the latter sentences of his address-dangers of inquisition at the hands of parliament, an inquisition embarrassing to the management itself, irritating to the personnel of the management, an inquisition designed for purposes wholly apart from any that go to the success of the system. Those who had to do with the initiation of the National Railways of Canada had some fear of just this thing. Early in its history we were subjected to exactly that style of inquisition. We were not surprised, but we stood in parliament and declared on oui responsibility as a government that it was our duty to lay down the rule which we would pursue, and to stand between such questioning and the directorate. We took the responsibility ourselves. We declared that questions that in any way affected the day to day management of the system, or that in any way embarrassed or prejudiced the management, would not be answered in this House. For taking that position we were arraigned throughout the length and breadth of Canada as autocrats, as men who sought to conceal,

CN.R.-Minister's Statement
as men who denied the representatives of the people those things to which they were justly entitled, and as men who wanted to hide, under some opaque monstrous substance, facts affecting over half the revenue and assets of the people of this Dominion. We had to stand that manner of attack. We were not subjected to that attack at the hands of the present Minister of Railways-he was not in the House-but at the hands of his leader chiefly, and at the hands of all his followers of that day. The hon. member for North Waterloo (Mr. Euler) shakes his head, and this time I have, as before, to make an exception in his case. He proved himself a friend of the National Railways early in its history, and I do not think he found fault with us for taking a stand which it was our duty to take, and which it has been for two and a half years the duty of this government to take, but which it had not the courage to assume. This government should have taken this stand and should have openly admitted that the late government was right, denied any inquisition and refused to answer a question which would prejudice the management in the discharge of its duty. They say that members should not ask questions. We do not depend on the will of members as to the management of this House. We have certain rules which all adopt, and we all follow the rule adopted and abide by it. Why not do it in regard to this matter as in other matters. Let the government take its own responsibility and refuse answers to questions which do not need to be answered for the good of parliament and which should not be answered for the good of the system.
Let me go to the other side of the picture which the minister did not refer to, and which I am sorry he did not take the trouble to discuss. Neither in office nor out of office have I subscribed to the principle that all the doings of the directors of the National Railways and the whole record of management should be a sealed book for all eternity. I have seen certain newspaper articles of recent date and some of older date that seemed to be inspired by that idea. There surely is some method by which all that the paanagement had done may be-subject perhaps to certain restraints, but very, very few -brought under the review of the committee of this House and under the review of parliament and shown up at such a time as in no way to embarrass the management or to interfere with the success of the operation of the system. Who is there who would suggest that the disposal of over half of the revenue of this Dominion, the honesty of that disposal,
the capacity or the inefficiency with which the whole thing is managed, must never be reviewed by the shareholders of the corporation and must be closed and relegated to the past; that we have to take the word of one single man, however mighty, that all is well find fine, and that if we attempt to review it and go very far back, we are treading on holy ground and must be prevented. But really that is the position we are in now.
I think there should be a standing committee of this House to which, for example, the report read to-day by the Minister of Railways could be submitted. We spend time here on the estimates of this department and that department; we pass votes for $100, $1,000, $10,000 and so on, we debate some of them for hours and all the while moneys by the millions, yea, by the hundreds of millions, are swiftly expended without our knowledge and we have nc concern about it. These moneys are paid out, discharged and disbursed by a directorate. We here in parliament, who are trustees for .that money in just the same sense, at least to just the same extent, as we are trustees for the rest of the money of the .people of Canada, have not one word to say and have not the right to review it.

Is not that a very strong argument for what was urged in this House some years ago by the hon. member for Shelburne and Queens (Mr. Fielding), that all the moneys collected for the National Railways should go into consolidated account and should be paid out under resolutions of this House, as other expenditures are paid out?

I do not think so, because when the hon. member urges this proposition he runs counter to the very sound principle which the Minister of Railways enunciated and advocated, but which the government has not the courage to enforce; namely the principle that such immediate and direct control on the part of parliament is inconsistent with the whole system of directorate management, and directorate management is essential to the business success of the enterprise. Some time must elapse before, in my judgment, anything can be fairly, equitably, safely, inquired into, and there may have to be some restraints as to inquiries even applying to matters further back. I can imagine cases where there would be. Something must be left to the directorate in the way of discretion, a prima facie case being made for them as a safeguard against perilous inquisition. But subject to that, all the expenditure of

this money, when it is through and done, should come before a committee of this House, and all the matters that are embraced, for example, in the annual presentations and monthly presentations of the concern should be studied carefully by members of this House. I want to review new some of the facts and figures brought out by the minister and by the president in - his report. Comparing the year 1923 with the year 1922, regard must be had to two or three very important considerations. Although, perhaps, the year 1922 might have been the same, certainly the condition could not have been the same before, but actually and necessarily in 1923, for the first time we had the advantages of an amalgamated system. We had the Grand Trunk railway and the National railways, the old Canadian Northern and the government railways, all operated as one entity instead of as two entities. That there would be economies and advantages in the way of one management by this amalgamation, everyone anticipated. I for one anticipated much greater economy than now appears in evidence. Perhaps, however, I had not ground for the anticipation. All I ask now is that hon. members consider that this advantage appertained to 1923 and is an infinitely greater advantage than all the rather picayune things referred to by the minister as unfavourable to the operations of that year. There is another feature. The year 1923, from a freight carrying standpoint, was the most abundant year we have ever known; 1923 witnessed a crop production of some 470,000,000 bushels, seventy million bushels more in this respect alone than that of any previous year. Consequently the railway got the benefit of the freight that resulted. These matters I draw attention to. I cannot think of any major factor favourable to the previous years as against 1923.
I come now to review the results. I do so. more in a spirit of examination and inquiry than in a spirit of criticism. I do not pretend to have had that very close association

Now I come to what I consider a more serious phase of the inquiry. No one would more like to find better results than I would myself, and I had hoped that we should get to that stage sooner than we are doing. The minister knows that we improved much faster that year; and that year showed a more rapid rate of improvement still over the preceding period. Similarly, the chances of the railways for immediate improvement after large sums are expended in the betterment of the system are rather better than they are going to be later on when more normal conditions are reached.

Every extra train load of wheat you draw adds the cost of hauling that load of wheat to the transportation expense, and the greater the amount of traffic hauled by the railways the greater the transportation expense.

That is correct. I never, even by inference, disputed that. In fact, I was trying to drive that home to the minister in respect of maintenance of cars and maintenance of ways. That is very true; it costs more to transport more goods. But here is the point: In respect of the improvement of the one year over the year before, in 1922

ove? 1921 it is virtually wholly due to reduction of this account, but in respect of 1923 over 1922 none of it is due to reduction; there is an increase, perhaps not very important when you take into account the increase in traffic. It is all due to maintenance of way and maintenance of equipment reduction. Surely the importance of this fact is clear to the minister.
Now I go further. I find that in 1922 there was a reduction in the payroll of $10,753,495, whereas in 1923 there was an increase of $7,714,273. I find many other details to which I could allude, but I do not think the occasion is proper for such an examination as the revelation of those details would entail.
Let me say this: The minister should very carefully go into all the accounts that are returned in the income statement of the Canadian National Railways, not only the minister and the government, but there should be a committee of this House to which these accounts would be submitted, a committee whose duty it would be to examine them thoroughly and acquaint the parliament of Canada with the real facts of the situation. Explanations of these accounts might possibly be given by the officials of the system. They would be very adequate explanations to satisfy me. There looks to me to be an unjust charge to capital, and an unfair reduction of charges to operation. On the face of the returns, at least that is evident. That may be only a prima facie conclusion that one comes to, but certainly it should be the duty of this House to examine fully and to know the inner meaning of all these returns, and know whether there is an answer to the indications which I have sought to convey to the House this afternoon. The desirability of such a committee must be manifest. We have a whole lot of standing committees now; we have had them added to this session, and I think we have some we could very well do without, some that I think are merely shunts, merely pieces of machinery by which initial responsibility in the government can be evaded. We could get rid of some of these standing committees, and then establish a committee which would have reposed in it a duty and a responsibility bigger than any standing committee of this House in the past ever discharged.

subtopic: SUPPLY ON THURSDAYS OR FRIDAYS IN CASE OF ADJOURNED DEBATE
speechtext:
The House is aware, I
have no doubt, that on Thursdays and Fridays when the Order of the Day is called for the House to go into committee of Supply as is the case to-day, or to go into committee of Ways and Means, the rule requires that the Speaker shall leave the chair without putting any question. On Wednesday evening the hon. member for West York (Sir Henry Drayton) moved the adjournment of the debate on the report, presented by the Minister of Railways, on the Canadian National Railways. If hon. members will consult section 180 of Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms they will see that it is incumbent 
upon the Speaker to obey standing Rule 17c and leave the chair without question being put on Thursdays and Fridays on going into committee of Supply or of Ways and Means. I quote the following from Section 180:
If an adjourned debate on such an amendment is standing upon the order paper when supply, for consideration of which in committee it is not necessary to propose the question for the Speaker's leaving the chair, is to be taken, the Order of the Day for resuming the adjourned debate is removed, and procedure on the amendment lapses, in order that the Speaker, in obedience to Rule 17c, may leave the chair without question put.
There is no amendment before the Chair at the present moment but there is a motion to adjourn the debate. Irrespective, however, of whether there is a motion or an amendment offered, on Thursdays and Fridays the Speaker must leave the chair without question put. The same rule obtains in England. Strangely enough, the point is stated in England in rule 17 while our own rule is 17c. I shall read the English rule:
Whenever the committee of supply stands as an order of the day, Mr. Speaker shall leave the chair without putting any question, unless on first going into supply on the army, navy, or civil service estimates respectively, or on any vote of credit, an amendment be moved, or question raised, relating to the estimates proposed to be taken into supply.
With reference to this, May, at page 476 has the following comment which I think may aptly be quoted:
If an adjourned debate on that question is standing upon the notice paper when supply, for the consideration of which in committee it is not necessary to propose the question for the Speaker's leaving the chair, is to be taken, the Order of the Day for resuming the adjourned debate is removed, and procedure on the amendment lapses, in order that the Speaker, in obedience to the standing order, may leave the chair without question put.
This of course does not preclude the hon. member from bringing up the question at another sitting when a formal motion is made, or, if the hon. member prefers to take another course, he may continue the debate upon an item being called in committee. That is optional with him. I simply desire to be clear on this point, however; the Speaker has no alternative on Thursdays and Fridays, when he must obey the standing rule and leave the chair without question put, upon the House going into committee of Supply or of Ways and Means.
