Mr. Chairman,
some remarks that I should like to make in regard to this item of hospitalization must be deferred until I receive those reports, because the information which I expect to get from them will have a bearing on what I am going to say. I will confine my remarks now to the subject of tubercular cases amongst ex-service men. I am very much interested in this because I fear that the experience which the first division had at the second battle of Ypres has very much to do with the condition of a great many ex-service men to-day. I am aware that the expert advice given to the department is that the gas employed by the Germans at the second battle of Ypres has very little to do with these tubercular cases. I am well aware that the gas which was let loose during thait weekx did not by any means carry over the tubercular bacilli to the men of the first division, but I do know that the injury those men then received should have very much to do with their physical condition in after years. Those medical men who were on duty at that time will remember the thousands of soldiers

Supply-Re-establishment

brought in suffering from the effects of gas. Such a thing had never been experienced in warfare before. Many men died' in the ambulances on the way to the hospitals, and many of those who survived and later were returned to the front dropped dead on the march back to the trenches. The injury to the respiratory tract was very severe, and in my opinion many of these men to-day are suffering from the effects of gas. It is quite true that no bacilli were carried over with that gas, but the mucous membrane of the respiratory tract was practically destroyed and the tract so weakened that after-effects would follow, such as bronchitis, and in many cases tuberculosis. The expert medical advisers of the Board of Pension Commissioners and the Department of Soldiers' Civil Reestablishment, I know, strongly advise against any connection between gas and tubercular cases. But I think I am safe in saying that no medical man can say definitely when tuberculosis began, it being very difficult to diagnose, even with the help of the X-ray and other technical means. I am in great sympathy with our ex-service men who are suffering from tuberculosis. They need the sympathy of the country, and I think that if a man is known at any time to have experienced the effects of poison gas he should be treated as having disability due to service, or at least aggravated by service. Many cases of tuberculosis are being thrown upon the country, and in the opinion of some medical men the disability is due to service, or aggravated by service, although the medical men of the department deny that there is any relation whatever between poison gas and tuberculosis. To-day some of these cases are being supported by the charity of the towns and cities where they live. Now Sir, we have only two institutions absolutely supported by the government for the treatment of exservice men suffering from tuberculosis, one being the institution known as the Mowat hospital in Kingston. This was started as a provincial organization by the Association of Health in the city of Kingston, which collected funds and, with support from the provincial government, founded the institution. It was taken over by the government during the war, and although it would be a great burden upon any health association to carry the work on, it is now proposed to turn this institution back to the organization which started it.
I think that the government instead of slowing up on this work should go forward. I asked the minister the other night if he was aware of the number at Gravenhurst. Last

fall there were 28 ex-service men at Gravenhurst suffering from tuberculosis, who, not coming under a designation of the act, were therefore receiving no support or aid. It would be very difficult for any medical officer, no matter how experienced he was, to say whether the condition of those men was due to service or was not. I suppose that in some cases the cause could be assigned, in others it could not. I think it would be only fair on the government's part to continue that work. Like the member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Carroll) I believe that the government perhaps acted too quickly in the closing of these institutions, and I would like to think that they had given the matter serious consideration before taking that aetidn. Some institution such as the minister has spoken of to-day should be maintained in centres like Kingston, Toronto and London to provide for the treatment of men in those districts. Sydenham hospital at Kingston was closed up and the minister made arrangements for the treatment of certain cases in the two general hospitals while others were dragged away to Toronto and Ste. Anne's for treatment. Conditions are not the same as they were some years ago We can remember the time in this country when men would leave their families, go away to the bush for six or seven months and know that their families would be taken care of. To-day such charitable conditions do not prevail in the cities and when men leave their families to go to distant centres like Toronto or Montreal they do so with a good deal of apprehension, not knowing what will happen to their families. I think the department has been a little careless in this matter; they take a long time to answer some letters and frequently the member for the district has to intervene to hurry up the correspondence. In some cases I have known these men to be in the institutions several months without any report being given or diagnosis made to determine whether or not they were getting any aid. The closing of Sydenham was just as much a hardship as this. Sydenham hospital was closed for two reasons. The first was, I think, that in that hospital there was a more favourable diagnosis of the cases than there was at some other places. In some instances I have had to check up the department in this respect. One instance I have in mind was a case in which the X-ray examination showed a very grievous condition. The man was sent to Toronto where men less favourable to the patient gave a less favourable report, which made a great deal of difference in his treatment. The second

Supply-Re-establishment
reason for the closing of Sydenham was pretty much a political reason. In the last election I secured a majority at Sydenham and the minister was besieged with correspondence to allow it to go and with requests also to remove the medical officers from the work- one officer in particular, Dr. Mundell, who on many occasions had been mentioned as the probable Liberal candidate but who for personal reasons supported me. This medical officer had given very long service to this country, first in the medical corps, then in the organization of the signal corps, and his boy came with me as a private to the Great War. For these personal reasons he gave me his support, and of course the minister was at once requested to behead him, which he did.
Before the Mowat hospital is closed I would like the minister to take into consideration the condition in which the men will be left. I pointed out to him at the time of the closing of Sydenham that the treatment in the military hospitals and the hospitals of the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment was different from that given in the general hospitals. The men are more at home in their own hospitals, and that psychological effect upon the men means a great deal in their treatment. I will admit that in general the treatment given by the department in their hospitals has been good and that complaint has arisen only in isolated cases. The trouble with the medical men is that they have made diagnoses in the past; they have got into a rut, and they are not big enough to admit their mistakes. Let me give you two examples. I have a picture here that I will send over to the minister, relating to a case which I had to force the department to consider. That is the picture of a young boy, the last of four sons of a Kingston family. The boy was in camp with me twice when very young; I never knew him to be sick in his life. He went overseas, reached England just about the time the war closed, and returned with an affection which developed just as the minister sees in that picture. The departmental headquarters refused to have anything to do with this case, but finally they were forced to take him in. He was sent to Sydenham and Toronto, and he died last year. Although there were three other boys he was the only support of his father and mother and he died without any help being given by the department. That case was seen by the medical men and it should have moved the heart of anybody to give him some assistance. Another case was one of rheumatism from 168i
which heart trouble developed. The young man was in hospital for treatment but was sent home, according to headquarters, because nothing more could be done for him. I visited the home of that man and I never saw a home so pitiful in my life. It was a straight case of heart disease resulting from rheumatism. They were finally forced to take him into hospital, where he died three weeks after admission. The report given on that case by medical men of the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment was that it was a new disease. But as I say it was nothing more than heart trouble following on rheumatism. My experience has, possibly, brought more of these ex-service men to me for help than to any other member of the House. In many cases I s.aw them at the front, I have seen them at home in the hospitals and 1 have had a great deal to do with them. Now, what is the trouble? The trouble is that the majority of the men are being well looked after and well cared for by this government. But, unfortunately, there is now a small minority of cases that have been diagnosed first one way and then another by the department, and because a mistake was made in the first place, they are not big enough to say now, "Here, we made a mistake," unless you absolutely force them to admit it with a heap of witnesses and other evidence. I admit that those who get treatment get good treatment, but I am going now to give what I think are a few of the troubles which no regulation and no appeal board seems to correct. They show what I would call a lack of sympathy in their attitude towards the men. They will tell you, and we have heard this on the committee very many times, that they are giving the men the benefit of the doubt. Well, I contend that the benefit of the doubt can only be given if in the case of two doctors differing, the man receives help in some way. But they do not give him the benefit of the doubt. If the department's doctor has given an opinion, no matter what the age and the experience of the doctor on the outside, the opinion of the department's doctor goes, and the man gets no benefit. I could give many instances of that. I think the trouble is that the doctors who are dealing with these cases at headquarters have not the experience they should have. I have asked some questions in regard to the medical men who are advising the department to-day. You would expect that they would be men of some length of experience, but what do you find? I asked the board for the length of service, the war record of
Supply-Re-establishment

these men, and I ascertained that out of nine advisers the chief one is an eye specialist. Now this is not the man to whom they refer their eye cases in Toronto. If the man comes down here he is generally referred to Dr. Courtenay. This chief adviser is an eye specialist, not a general service man. There are two others who were not graduates in medicine at the time of the war, but who have since graduated, and that is their only experience. Now these are not the men who should advise against men of long service. Let me give you an example. I have repeatedly taken the advice of Dr. W. T. Connell, of Kingston. This man was for years the pathologist at Queen's University, a man known as a pathologist not only in Canada but all over the United States, one of the big men in the medical line in Canada. To-day he is at the head of Medicine at Queen's University. Now that man's opinion is constantly being contradicted by men who have graduated since the war, and who have had no other experience, and I think that is one reason why the men who have disabilities suffer.
There are two or three very particular cases that I would like to take up, just to show how the opinions of these men collide. There is the case of a man who enlisted in Chicago in the last year of the war. He came over to Canada, went overseas, and returned with a nerve disability. The man cannot do any work. He had no disability of this kind when he went overseas, but he has this disability now. Now, you can see, it becomes a matter of opinion as between neurologists, one neurologist saying that this man's disability must be due to a sickness which occurred on service, and the other saying that he can find no connection whatever; it is simply a matter of opinion. Finally I got the reason of the man whose opinion was taken. He said that as the arm showed no lessening in size and so on, therefore the trouble could not amount to anything. But here is a man who was well when he went overseas, and who was returned with this disability, and to-day he is walking the streets. The minister and his department have known that eases of this kind have existed for over a year, and yet no recommendation has been brought in as to how they are going to take care of such cases in the future. Let me add that this man on Christmas Day was asked by some ex-service men if he had any place to go to. Having none, but being ashamed to say No, he said, Yes, he had a good place to go to, and he walked the streets all day. We have tried to keep him in the hospital and

help him outside the hospital as well. Now a case of this kind does more harm to the department than- can be offset by the thousands of cases where they give good treatment. I do not like to bring the thing up as a straight criticism of the department, because I find the department doing a great many things to help; but there is no question that a mistake was made in regard to this man at the beginning; and men like Dr. Connell, who hrs observed this man for over two years and is satisfied that he has a case, have to see their opinion thrown on the scrap heap and the advice of the younger man taken.
There is another thing that causes a lot of trouble. The department answer you, very often, according to some record they have on the man's file, a record that perhaps shows the man misbehaved at some time; and that has a lot to do with the attitude they take towards him. Let me give the House one or two examples of what I mean. About two years ago I took up with the department here the case of a young fellow who had come into Kingston off the farm where he had worked about a year. That man has a great wound over the sciatic nerve; so that he has what is known to medical men as a drop foot; but it has been repaired to a certain extent. After working on the farm for about a year he came into Kingston to get some treatment or help of some kind. I wrote to the department, because the man had obtained no answer in regard to his case. In their first letter to me the department said that this man was a bootlegger. I took all the means I could of investigating that charge, and found that there was no justification for it whatever. Then I wrote the department and asked them to confirm their charge that this man was a bootlegger, because if he was, I did not care to have much to do with him. They answered that they could not understand why they had made such a charge; there was no evidence against the man. The facts were that this man had been sent to work with his brother-in-law, and they had had a quarrel, and now he was thrown back on the hands of the department. I investigated the charge and found there was no ground for it. About two pages of foolscap were occupied with apologies and expressions of surprise at how this second charge came to be instituted. It was a shame that that man was allowed to engage in farm work. Crippled as he was, with dragging feet how was it to be expected that he could make his way across ploughed fields or fields of stubble? Yet that was the kind of treatment meted out to this man who went overseas and fought for his country.

Another thing in regard to these cases: Unless the medical officer has experience and knows what relation the injury has to the man's ability to work, great injustice is likely to be suffered by the latter. A physician who would make a report on this kind of case and expect the person to go out and work on a farm must have had very little experience in the ability of a man with such an injury to obtain work.
Some time ago a case was brought up of a man who had received a wound in the back that penetrated through to the front, producing a scar of fully twelve inches, with a great amount of injury to the tissues. Now, that man was supposed to be suffering from only fifteen per cent disability whereas it was a matter for wonder that he could work at all. The opinion of practitioners of experience should be obtained in such cases instead of applying to men who have only graduated since the war. Some of these men went overseas as corporals and sergeants, and afterwards were sent; back to complete their medical studies. Instead of employing persons of such limited experiences as that, as I pointed out last year, the department should secure the biggest medical men obtainable in Canada for the treatment of these afflicted soldiers.
Now, as to the treatment of tubercular cases: Instead of abandoning this work the department should extend the regulations so as to take in cases with which they do not deal at the present time. I maintain that before finally disposing of the Mowat sanatorium, which is one of the two special treatment hospitals, the department should go further into the matter and see whether or not the operations of such institutions should not be extended, not left to a small group of men and women who are sacrificing a great deal to carry on this work at the present, time.
In the next place I think the department should cut out one feature to be found in its regulations in regard to the treatment of disabilities other than those produced by war. The minister and his deputy are well acquainted with the case I am going to describe. It was that of a man who had a disability of so much per cent arising from varicose veins and hernia produced by the war. This man was getting on very well, with his pension and the work he had to do:	He was a gardener and was making a
very good living. One day he reported for examination before the department. He was taken to Sydenham hospital, but a fire occurred and he was sent from there to St.
Anne's, Montreal. There without consulting him they operated twice on his feet for overlapping toes, a condition that was not specially due to war. It was a condition with which the authorities should not have interfered at all. If they did not operate for a condition not due to war then the question of responsibility properly arose. This man, as I say, had a small pension and at first was able to work. But they operated twice on his teet, and the result is that his toes are absolutely rigid. He cannot work, he can get no employment whatever, and the department refuses to accept any responsibility for his case. The man was removed to St. Anne's away from his home and family, away from any of his relatives or friends with whom he could consult. These two operations were performed and to-day his case is absolutely hopeless. He cannot walk, his toes are rigid and stiff as a result of these two operations, and whenever he tries to walk he falls down. That is another case of the kind I am describing. It is a case which does more harm to the department than thousands of good cases in which benefit has resulted to the persons concerned. I am told that in this particular case only intervention prevented a third operation. At any rate the man was sent home helpless to his family.

I hesitate to discuss at all any question involving medical knowledge; but I want to bring to the attention of the minister the case of an ex-soldier,-and I shall have no hesitation in mentioning his name, because the case has been the subject of comment in the public press. I do this for the purpose of indicating what appears to me to be in some way or another a lack of co-ordination or cooperation amongst the various bodies concerned with the welfare of disabled soldiers. This soldier had his case considered by the Great War Veterans' Association, and I asked the secretary of that association to give me a memorandum detailing the facts. The soldier's name is H. S. Liddell:
This man enlisted in the 181st Battalion on May 29, 1916, at Brandon, Manitoba. He was aged 39, and it was subsequently discovered that he had suffered mental disturbances on two occasions prior to enlistment. He served with the Canadian Expeditionary Force approximately three years of which eleven and oneehalf months were spent in France. Liddell came to Canada in February 1910, and made homestead entry. Upon discharge from the Canadian Expeditionary Force in June, 1919, he made an effort to resume farming activities. His mother joined him during the

same year, but found to her amazement that her son was not mentally competent. His condition rapidly grew worse until it became necessary to report him to the authorities.
Within eleven months after discharge, in May, 1920, he was placed under treatment by the Department of Soldiers' Civil Reestablishment, finally being committed to Selkirk asylum. He was released on probation in April, 1921, while under observation during this outbreak, he was examined and reported upon by a number of medical men, at least three of whom were mental specialists. It was unanimously agreed that this condition had been aggravated by service to the extent of 25 per cent. The department accepted responsibility for treatment and awarded allowances to the dependent mother.
In August, 1922, it was reported that Liddell had suffered another outbreak, necessitating institutional care. On this occasion, the department denied all responsibility stating that the disability was of a constitutional nature, and that there had 'been no mental episode recorded on service'; a finding quite contradictory to the original finding upon which treatment had been awarded. The mother was given employment escorting a female patient to England. During her absence in England and without her knowledge, the son was deported. Since that time, she has been in Canada in destitute circumstances and conflicting reports have been received about the welfare of Liddell himself in England. In any event, it is quite clear from medical evidence that he is not mentally stable, although, I understand, he is of a quiet disposition.
I am frank to say that these matters have been brought to the attention of the minister on several occasions, I believe. The deputy minister and the director of medical services have always been insistent that the department could not accept responsibility for institutional care, for the reasons already stated. The minister, however, finally concurred in an order for repatriation. ,
Meanwhile, the case was brought to appeal before the appeal board and in 'December, 1923, the appeal of the soldier was sustained. A special appeal was made to the minister by the representatives of the Great War Veterans' Association that, in view of the destitution of the mother, the department should not exercise its right to enter re-appeal. It was pointed out that a reasonable doubt in favour of the appellant had been established. On December 19, 1923, however, the department was committed by the deputy minister to reappeal. In the meantime, the minister was good enough to provide that special relief be

Supply-Re-establishment
extended to the mother. As it was evident that several months would elapse before a quorum of the board could be assembled in Winnipeg, the soldiers' adviser waived the right of personal appearance on behalf of Mrs. Liddell and deputized Mr. MacNeil, in this city to act on her behalf at the hearing of the re-appeal. The re-appeal was heard in Ottawa on January 31, 1924, and was rejected, judgment being given in favour of the appellant, that is the soldier, on February 7, 1924. Again, the department was urged to take immediate action to afford Mrs Liddell relief by adjustment of pay and allowances for which her eligibility had been established by the appeal board.
Steps were then taken to determine whether or not pension was indicated as apparently medical treatment was not necessary at all times. Inquiry was made of the Board of Pension Commissioners as to whether or not judgment of the appeal board respecting the eligibility for medical treatment would be accepted in regard to award of pension. On March 29th, however, the board gave the decision:	Refusing pension
payments to this soldier on the ground that his mental condition existed prior to enlistment, was wilfully concealed on enlistment and was aggravated during service to a negligible extent only. I am informed that the form in which the decision of the Board of Pension Commissioners was given has prevented any further appeal in the matter of pension before the federal appeal board. Aggravation is assumed, but it is described as negligible, and there is no appeal.
The thing that the ordinary individual cannot understand, at least that I cannot understand, is this. This man was accepted for service. If he were mentally unfit, it is a wonder at the time of examination for service that fact was not discovered by the Militia department's officers. The man, it was said, wilfully concealed these facts, but at the same time I presume the man was quite satisfied with his medical condition. He certainly would not go abroad parading his insanity before the public. All the difficulties-the attitude of the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment in constantly referring this matter back, seeking apparently any avenue of excuse in order to escape payment and the failure of the Board of Pension Commissioners to accept the final judgment of the appeal board in the matter and suggesting that the aggravation, if any, due to service, was only negligible, thus denying the right of the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment at the outset to pay any
compensation whatever, are things which, frankly, I do not understand. It seems to me that if the minister has not already considered these matters, steps should be taken to co-ordinate these departments and to get them working together. I understand that a soldier may receive pay and allowances and treatment from the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment, but that when he comes to the pension board to ask for a pension, it is like going to an entirely different government. He has to make a new appeal. The pension board do not recognize,-I am informed; I do not know- that there is such a thing as the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment. There must be something wrong which allows a case, particularly of this character, to go on in the condition in which it has gone on for so many months and finally to wind up with a soldier in this country being deported, I presume, as an undesirable, and his mother being deported also in order to be with her son. I do not mention these facts in a spirit of criticism; I draw this matter to the attention of the minister and the committee which is considering soldiers' problems simply because if these facts are true-and they are given to me as true-they are disgraceful and should not be tolerated for a single moment.

I desire to say just a few words on the question of hospital administration more particularly in view of statements that have been made in the early part of this year concerning the suggested change of policy of the department which would remove from the executive head of the hospitals the medical professional men who now serve as superintendents and replace them by laymen, I cannot say to what extent this new policy has been carried out nor to what extent, indeed, it has been decided upon. I believe the committee will be interested in hearing from the minister on this point. I understand, however, that in the case of Ste. Anne de Bellevue hospital a layman has been appointed as superintendent in place of the medical man who formerly had charge of the institution. In any case this policy has created considerable unrest among medical officers in the Dominion and in the medical profession generally. I was asked to attend1 a meeting which was held in February of this year to consider the question, and I believe that similar meetings have been held in various parts of the Dominion. The meeting crystallized its action in a telegram which was sent to the minister (Mr. Belaud), and various other ministers of the government, as well as to the director of medical services. This telegram, which is dated February 5, of this year and despatched from St. John, New Brunswick, reads:
At a meeting of the medical profession held in St. John, New Brunswick, February 5, 1924, Doctor J. H. Allingham, president of New Brunswick Medical Association being in the chair, the following resolution was adopted.
"It having been brought to the attention of the medical profession that it is the intention of the gov-vemment to make an alteration in the form of management of the D.S.C.It. whereby the supreme authority shall be placed in the hands of laymen in the administrative department and that the office of the medical superintendent in hospitals is about to bp abolished and laymen appointed in their places, the profession desires to place upon record its entire disapproval of any such proposed action feeling that it will strike at the root of medical efficiency in the treatment of returned soldiers without presenting any compensatory returns."
E. J. Ryan.
Similar action I understand was taken in other parts of the country in reference to this matter and I hope that the minister will give us some information as to what, if any, change has taken place in the policy of the department in view of this representation which has been submitted to him.
My attitude has been, and is, favourable towards the department, because in the first place I think this is due the department, and secondly, because I feel that one must 
be very careful not to impair the confidence of the men receiving treatment from the department unless it is well established that there exists grounds for criticising that treatment. On the whole I do not criticise it, and I do not refer to the matter with a view to condemning the department, that is not my attitude; I believe it is my duty to maintain the confidence of the men in the department. Here, however, is a question that does affect the treatment of the soldiers. If it be true that it is proposed to put laymen in charge of these institutions then, though possibly we may be engaging men at a smaller salary, we are certainly appointing those who cannot have the same intimate knowledge of the subject and who naturally therefore must be less capable than the professional men who formerly, and still to a considerable extent have had charge of the hospitals. My view is that in the diminution of officials in the Department of Soldiers' Civil Reestablishment the extra professional members of the staff should be the first to go; and as the lessening process continues the dismissals should be made from the non-professional rather than from the professional side. The question must always necessarily be a medical one, and largely so. Whatever the size of the department may be at any particular time, the work must be pre-eminently of a medical nature. So that I urge the minister to consider this question seriously; for while I agree that it is proper to reduce the staff as far as it is necessary to do so, I am strongly of the opinion that those who are allowed to go should be selected from among the non-professional members of the staff.

Mr. Chairman, just a
word in reply to the remarks that have been made by the hon. member for Kingston, the hon. member for West Calgary, the hon. member for St. John, and the hon. member who has just taken his seat (Mr Manion). I may say that I am accepting the remarks that have been made in the spirit in which they have been presented to the House. I realize that it 'is constructive criticism of a work which everybody will admit is extremely involved and difficult.
A number of individual cases have been referred to. Undoubtedly more individual cases could be cited to the House as an example either of lack of efficiency or lack of sympathy on the part of medical officials and other officials of the department. It is very true, as has been properly stated by the hon. member for Kingston, that one case of hardship draws more criticism and causes more discontent amongst the population than a thousand cases which are dealt with satisfactorily. If the committee will bear with me for a moment I will just give a few figures, from memory, to show to what an extent the work of this department is carried on. The department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment has to-day on its books 63,000 pensioners; 43,000 soldiers who are suffering from a disability are receiving a pension, and in round figures 20,000 dependents, mainly widows and widowed mothers. So that if you should find in this country fifty cases of men or widows who are refused pensions, it would not be such a very large proportion compared with the total number who have been awarded a pension. I agree entirely with what has been said, that if it is at ail possible, no mistake should be made, no injustice, not even the slightest, should be done by the department. This figure I have given, 63,000, represents only pensioners. Consider also, for a moment, the number of men who are treated in one year. Leaving aside the 3,360 men who are now receiving active treatment in hospitals, the department has treated 167,000 times during the year men who have seen service at the front or who have been engaged in the army in any branch. So that in the treatment section also, if a few men are refused treatment when they claim they

are entitled to it, though it is regrettable if an injustice is done, the proportion refused treatment compared with the total number who have received fair treatment is not in any way too large. But still my efforts have been directed always towards this goal, that any man who has the remotest ground upon which to base a claim for pension or treatment should receive pension or treatment.
Now let us make a distinction between the Board of Pension Commissioners and the department itself, that is, that part of the department which deals with treatment. The Board of Pension Commissioners is a tribunal constituted by a statute of this parliament as an independent tribunal, as independent of me, or for that matter of you, Mr. Chairman, and the members of this House, as the Supreme Court of Canada. I cannot direct, and no minister before me could, and if the statute is not changed, no minister after me can, direct the board to award or refuse a pension, or to increase or decrease a pension. It is absolutely beyond me.

subtopic: SUPPLY ON THURSDAYS OR FRIDAYS IN CASE OF ADJOURNED DEBATE
speechtext:
Will the minister
permit questions as he goes along; otherwise certain points may be lost sight of. We are. I think, proceeding in a good-natured way.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
subtopic: SUPPLY ON THURSDAYS OR FRIDAYS IN CASE OF ADJOURNED DEBATE
speechtext: Certainly, at any time.

subtopic: SUPPLY ON THURSDAYS OR FRIDAYS IN CASE OF ADJOURNED DEBATE
speechtext: The Board of Pension Commissioners, of course, has the decision, but it is made on the advice of these medical men, and these nine men that I refer to are serving the Board of Pension Commissioners and also the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment, with the exception of the units. I was directing my criticism to that.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
subtopic: SUPPLY ON THURSDAYS OR FRIDAYS IN CASE OF ADJOURNED DEBATE
speechtext:
There are a number of
medical men, of course, who, as my hon. friend suggests, have to do with both the treatment section and the pension section, but the Board of Pension Commissioners have a body of medical men to themselves, with which I have nothing to do in any way, shape or form; there are nine of them, I think.

subtopic: SUPPLY ON THURSDAYS OR FRIDAYS IN CASE OF ADJOURNED DEBATE
speechtext: These are the nine I spoke of?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
subtopic: SUPPLY ON THURSDAYS OR FRIDAYS IN CASE OF ADJOURNED DEBATE
speechtext:
Exactly; we have nothing
to do with the medical advisers of the Board of Pension Commissioners. They select their own advisers, and out of deference to them I never interfere with their selections. I coud not impose on them a medical man as their adviser. They are an independent tribunal, and they have nine medical men

Supply-Re-establishment
But outside of these nine medical men who are attached to the board, there are a number of medical men in every great city of Canada, and here at headquarters, over whom I have some jurisdiction. I could remove them all;
I could replace them all; but I may say that since I have been in that department I do not think I have changed five of these men. They were there before, and if I am well informed, and I am subject to correction by my hon. friend, they are amongst the most outstanding in the medical profession of Canada. Just for the sake of enlightening the committee, I will give the names of a few of the men who are consulted in Toronto in connection with the disabilities and diseases of soldiers. I have here the list. I do not know any of these men personally, but I am told that they are among the most outstanding medical men in the city of Toronto. There are for instance, Dr. Martin, Dr. Curtis, Dr. Gilchrist, Dr. Fletcher, Dr. Norwich, Dr. Starr, Dr. Boyer, Dr. Pentecost, Dr. Ryerson, Dr. Shenstone, Dr. Maclaurin, Dr. Gunn, Dr. Cole, Dr. Murray, Dr. Clare, Dr. Lemesurier. These men have their specialties. Some of them are medical advisers, some are surgeons, some neurologists, some nose and throat specialists, some chest specialists, exclusively, and so on. I have many times myself asked the director of medical services, "You rely upon the opinion of these men, but are they outstanding in their profession, are they absolutely reliable in a professional sense?" And every time the answer given me was: "These men are amongst the most prominent of the profession," and I have never heard anything to the contrary. I agree with my hon. friend from Kingston that the medical gentleman to whom he referred is also an outstanding specialist in Kingston.

subtopic: SUPPLY ON THURSDAYS OR FRIDAYS IN CASE OF ADJOURNED DEBATE
speechtext: I suppose the minister understands my criticism. It was the opinion of this outstanding man who went up to the board that was turned down by men who did not have anything like his experience.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
subtopic: SUPPLY ON THURSDAYS OR FRIDAYS IN CASE OF ADJOURNED DEBATE
speechtext:
No doubt some of these
cases happen, and I regret that, as my hon. friend does, but all I can do is to direct the criticism to the board, and they say to me as they would say to my hon. friend if he were the minister, "You have no jurisdiction; we are interpreting the statute."

subtopic: SUPPLY ON THURSDAYS OR FRIDAYS IN CASE OF ADJOURNED DEBATE
speechtext: That is true of the pension board, but not of the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
subtopic: SUPPLY ON THURSDAYS OR FRIDAYS IN CASE OF ADJOURNED DEBATE
speechtext:
I am coming to that.
When treatment is refused to a man we are
entirely responsible. If a mistake has been made in refusing treatment to a returned soldier, I am to blame, or my officials under me, and I suppose I am responsible for them, though I must admit that only a very small proportion of individual cases come before the minister; but however small is that proportion, there is not one day in the year but I examine personally ten different files, and as my hon. friend (Mr. Manion) who has had experience in this line knows, it is extremely long, involved, and intricate work to draw a file, which may be two inches thick. Well, we have to go into them. I have been delving into them day after day, and I think in most cases we have been able to adjust matters. As I said a year ago, medical science is not exact, and it will take a long time before it is exact. It has nothing in common with mathematics. Doctors disagree, and it is exceedingly difficult in some cases to say in any definite manner that a man is suffering from a disability that is related to his war service. In every case my instructions have been to this effect:	Where there is a doubt, give
treatment, if not with pay and allowances, without pay and allowances. We have some jurisdiction in this connection. We have a large number of men who are under treatment without pay and allowances, because there is nothing which would indicate that their malady or their disease is related to their war service, except in a very remote manner, and the consensus of medical opinion is that it is not related to service.

subtopic: SUPPLY ON THURSDAYS OR FRIDAYS IN CASE OF ADJOURNED DEBATE
speechtext: I agree that there are cases such as the minister speaks of, and this one I cited was one of them which probably should have been given treatment on the off-chance that the disability was due to service. That was all I ever asked for, an investigation; I never asked for anything else. But the minister's officials took exactly the same stand in that case also-and that is the argument I am making. They not only took the same stand but misquoted me by stating that I had asked for pay and allowances when I never had done anything of the kind. In cases where doubt exists it should be the duty of the department to put the man in the hospital and give him a little treatment. After all, it only means a very small amount of money to the Dominion of Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
subtopic: SUPPLY ON THURSDAYS OR FRIDAYS IN CASE OF ADJOURNED DEBATE
speechtext:
My hon. friend is quite right as regards the individual oases he has quoted. I remember very well the long correspondence there was in this particular case and ultimately, happily, I was induced
Supply-Re-establishment

to direct that this man should be treated. The opinion of Dr. Bruce was a very weighty one, and I came to the conclusion that we should yield. Very well, we have yielded.
Another case which has been brought to the attention of the committee is that of Liddell. I have not the file before me and have not looked at it for a long time. I knew the facts of the case perfectly at an earlier date, but I do not think I am 'thoroughly conversant with the circumstances at the moment. The case is a pathetic one inasmuch as the man was deported. Immediately I had learned of the deportation I took steps to have the Immigration department reconsider its decision. The department said the man had unwittingly been deported and his repatriation was ordered immediately, but he did not avail himself of the terms of the order. The widowed mother was awarded pay and allowances by the department and these were also made retroactive. I think we have adjusted this case. The question ' is asked why this man was refused treatment or a pension in the first place. Well, the refusal was based on the ground that before enlistment he suffered from the disabilities he was complaining of at the moment. That was the general ground for the refusal. Was the disability aggravated during service? Well, the Board of Pension Commissioners said no, or only to a negligible extent.

subtopic: SUPPLY ON THURSDAYS OR FRIDAYS IN CASE OF ADJOURNED DEBATE
speechtext: Was it not admitted that there was some aggravation of disability due to service and on that account was not a pension granted based on 25 per cent disability?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
subtopic: SUPPLY ON THURSDAYS OR FRIDAYS IN CASE OF ADJOURNED DEBATE
speechtext:
I was not aware of that. At any rate, the case has been adjusted. It is a pathetic ease and was the subject of a great deal of comment in conversation among the public and in the press.
Mr, ROSS (Kingston): Was the refusal of treatment in the 'Liddell case due to the fact that he was supposed to be mentally deficient previously?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
subtopic: SUPPLY ON THURSDAYS OR FRIDAYS IN CASE OF ADJOURNED DEBATE
speechtext: Yes, that was a ground.

speechtext:
The same as in
the Stoplin case. The department found the man a little deficient mentally but he was considered sane enough for service overseas. There were probably many others in the same condition, and I do not think it right to make that one of the reasons for a refusal to grant treatment or pension.

speechtext: Is the unit medical director any more efficient than the superintendent of the hospital.

I am coming to that in

It was a case that lent itself more than any other institution would do to this experiment. Captain Boyd lived in Ste. Anne; he could attend in the morning at the hospital, have a conference with the three or four medical men there, and in the afternoon he could discharge his duties in the unit office. That has been going on for the last three months with a good deal of satisfaction. He has reduced the staff expenditure, I understand, by $35,000 or $40,000 a year, and I am informed and, after having visited the hospital, I have been able to satisfy myself also, that the efficiency of the work has not at all suffered. There is an atmosphere of contentment in the hospital.

subtopic: SUPPLY ON THURSDAYS OR FRIDAYS IN CASE OF ADJOURNED DEBATE
speechtext: Was the same proposal not considered as regards the Mowat sanatorium?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
subtopic: SUPPLY ON THURSDAYS OR FRIDAYS IN CASE OF ADJOURNED DEBATE
speechtext:
No. In connection with the Mowat sanatorium, the hon. member for Kingston, in his able criticism of our work, has asked us to consider the matter very carefully before we decide to close that institution. He pointed out that we had only two T.B. institutions under the department. That is true as regards institutions entirely operated by the department; but may I point out that we have patients in other institutions throughout Canada? For instance if we take only the largest, we have at Hamilton at a sanatorium called Mountain, 75 T.B. patients, that is, on the strength. We have at London, Ontario, in Byron Sanatorium, 144 ex-soldier
Supply-Re-establishment

patients suffering from tuberculosis. We have other institutions with a smaller number of tubercular patients. It is true, as my hon. friend has stated, that we have only two T.B. institutions operated by the department, one at Calgary and one at Kingston.. The intention was to release Mowat sanatorium, because the number of our patients there declines year by year, month by month. We have come down now to 91 patients and we thought that the expenditure of the department could be reduced if we closed the institution or surrendered it to its owners. I may mem tion that I had a conference yesterday with the President of the Health Association at Kingston, a gentleman with whom the hon. member for Kingston is well acquainted. He was in Ottawa, and I had a conference with the deputy minister, the director of medical services and himself. I think we shall be able to arrive at a satisfactory arrangement in this connection, an arrangement to which, I think, my hon. friend will be in a position to give his support. The details are not yet entirely worked out, but I presume everybody in Kingston will be satisfied, my hon. friend the first. It will be possible for the institution to remain going and, I think, to be improved in this regard; more civilians will be treated there and the department will not overlook the good services it could render in this connection.

subtopic: SUPPLY ON THURSDAYS OR FRIDAYS IN CASE OF ADJOURNED DEBATE
speechtext: May I ask the name of the gentleman with whom the minister had the conference, or is it confidential?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
subtopic: SUPPLY ON THURSDAYS OR FRIDAYS IN CASE OF ADJOURNED DEBATE
speechtext: Dr. Connell was the gentleman with whom we had a conference yesterday.

subtopic: SUPPLY ON THURSDAYS OR FRIDAYS IN CASE OF ADJOURNED DEBATE
speechtext: Did I understand the minister to say that he had no jurisdiction over the pension board?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
subtopic: SUPPLY ON THURSDAYS OR FRIDAYS IN CASE OF ADJOURNED DEBATE
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: SUPPLY ON THURSDAYS OR FRIDAYS IN CASE OF ADJOURNED DEBATE
speechtext:
Is there any wtay of amending the act so that the minister would have some jurisdiction? In regard to the case in Winnipeg that the hon. member for Port William and Rainy River (Mr. Manion) mentioned, I have been to the minister and he tells me that he is without power. This woman has her pension cut off and she is charged with immoral conduct. So far as my information goes, that is absolutely wrong, the woman's character is above reproach. If the act is such that the minister has no jurisdiction and the pension board wants to be an autocratic body, there is no reason why this parliament should not amend the act so that cases of this kind may be reconsidered. In

this case they do not want to reinstate the pension although the woman's character has been defamed. There is no reason why the minister should not bring down the necessary amendments to meet this situation.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
subtopic: SUPPLY ON THURSDAYS OR FRIDAYS IN CASE OF ADJOURNED DEBATE
speechtext: There is no doubt that any act at all is subject to change; parliament is all powerful and can pass or amend acts as it pleases. Parliament, no doubt, might decree that I should be the sole dispenser of pensions. But if parliament did that I would resign immediately, for I do not want to be Minister of Pensions. I have no jurisdiction in this particular, and frankly I think it is better that it should be so. I do not think that a minister of the Crown should have the sole power of determining whether any pension should be granted, because too many considerations of a personal and political nature might be introduced to interfere with the discharge of his responsibilities.

subtopic: SUPPLY ON THURSDAYS OR FRIDAYS IN CASE OF ADJOURNED DEBATE
speechtext:
Not even after the
charge had been proved unfounded?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
subtopic: SUPPLY ON THURSDAYS OR FRIDAYS IN CASE OF ADJOURNED DEBATE
speechtext: I am coming to that. The case my hon. friend refers to is one that has been touched upon also by the hon. member for Fort William and Rainy River, and I am familiar with it. I am of the opinion that this pension should be reinstated and I have expressed that view to the Board of Pension Commissioners. They had information to the effect that the woman was living immorally and under the act they had power to suspend the pension. And this they did. Afterwards, a close investigation having been made by officials of the department and employees in Winnipeg, it was reported that the allegations appeared to be groundless, and it seems to me therefore that the pension should have been reinstated immediately. That it will be reinstated I have no doubt, although I have not received any information to the effect either that it has been refused or that it has been reinstated.

subtopic: SUPPLY ON THURSDAYS OR FRIDAYS IN CASE OF ADJOURNED DEBATE

Will the minister look
that matter up to-night?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
subtopic: SUPPLY ON THURSDAYS OR FRIDAYS IN CASE OF ADJOURNED DEBATE
speechtext: I will.

subtopic: SUPPLY ON THURSDAYS OR FRIDAYS IN CASE OF ADJOURNED DEBATE
speechtext:
It has been a great pleasure to listen to the ingenious way in which the minister makes his explanations;
I want to congratulate him on the way he does it.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
subtopic: SUPPLY ON THURSDAYS OR FRIDAYS IN CASE OF ADJOURNED DEBATE
speechtext: Thank you.

speechtext:
I regret, however, that there are not present more of his colleagues, who I am sure would benefit

Supply-Re-establishment
largely by paying close attention to the excellent performance of the Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; the hon. member would give a whole lot of them very useful instruction. It seems to me though that in some instances the minister might be more specific. We have heard of a case to-day which seems to be perfectly extraordinary; and while I would not want to trouble the minister with a request for specific details, it seems to me that if the rule as stated by the hon. member for Kingston (Mr. Ross) is applicable in the case of this gardener who had two operations performed upon him as a result of which he has lost his limbs, then a very serious hardship indeed exists. Simply because the loss by this man of the use of his limbs was not the result of war service, there is no reason why he should be entirely without recourse when he has been injured in this way through the carelessness or the malpractice of the department's doctors. If this rule is really the rule, it strikes me as being stupid, contrary to common sense and, what is more, inhuman. A man's usefulness in life is taken from him as a result of negligence, or worse, on the part of the doctors of the department, and I cannot see why in such circumstances he ought not to be looked after. Why, it is a most extraordinary situation, and my hon. friend has not dealt with it. Just consider the case for a moment. Here is a man who has served overseas and come back. He is suffering from some disability; he is working as a gardener in order to support himself and his family. In obedience to the rules of the department he is bound to report for inspection and for whatever other purpose the department may have in view. He is in receipt of a small pension by means of which, together with the proceeds of his work as a gardener, he is able to keep his family and support himself; and upon orders from the department he goes to the hospital. For what purpose? What is the underlying purpose? The real object is to cure him if possible so that he may no longer be a liability to the department. My hon. friend will correct me if I am wrong. That works a twofold benefit: if the man recovers he is of greater use to himself and the department is better off in consequence. Well, this man leaves his garden and puts himself in the hands of the departmental doctors; he has two operations and is discharged helpless. And then he is told that he has no possible remedy. I can hardly believe this to be true; indeed, I do not believe it is; it seems to me it could not possibly be so. The very 169
least that can be done for the man is to treat him with as much generosity as the present law will allow. See what the situation would be if this man had suffered similarly at the hands of private practitioners. He would be entitled to such damages as would take care of him for life; he would receive such an annuity as would enable him to live as nearly as possible in the condition he enjoyed before he was rendered useless as a result of malpractice on the part of the department's medical officers. I would ask the minister to look into the case carefully and to assure the committee that what has been cited to us as the rule of the department is not really true; so that when soldiers go to hospitals for treatment they will know that they are safe. If, on the instructions of the department, a man goes to a hospital to undergo an operation and the operation turns out a failure, surely that man should not be deprived of some compensation simply because the injury he sustains is not the result of war service, seeing that he has suffered in consequence of official malpractice. I hope the minister will reassure the committee on this point.

subtopic: SUPPLY ON THURSDAYS OR FRIDAYS IN CASE OF ADJOURNED DEBATE
speechtext:
As a matter of principle
my hon. friend is right; if the department through its medical officers is responsible for any injury it should assume that responsibility. In this case however, if I am well informed, the man suffered from varicose veins and was brought to Ste. Anne de Bellevue hospital. There he was treated by Dr. Gurd of Montreal who, while I am not personally acquainted with him, is well known by repute, being an outstanding surgeon. He decided to operate on the man, but only after the man had given his full consent.

subtopic: SUPPLY ON THURSDAYS OR FRIDAYS IN CASE OF ADJOURNED DEBATE
speechtext: What would he know about it?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
subtopic: SUPPLY ON THURSDAYS OR FRIDAYS IN CASE OF ADJOURNED DEBATE
speechtext: Perhaps he did not know very much; I agree with that. Whether the case has developed to such a pitiable extent or not, I am not aware. My hon. friend from Kingston says that the man is now unable to attend to the work which he was performing before. All I can say is that I shall make a note of the case and look into, it with every sympathy.

subtopic: SUPPLY ON THURSDAYS OR FRIDAYS IN CASE OF ADJOURNED DEBATE
speechtext:
Will my hon.
frined also do a little more; will he find out whether there is a rule which says there is to be no liability on the department in such a case? It does seem to me that that is something which ought to be dropped.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
subtopic: SUPPLY ON THURSDAYS OR FRIDAYS IN CASE OF ADJOURNED DEBATE
speechtext:
I will.

Supply-Re-establishment

subtopic: SUPPLY ON THURSDAYS OR FRIDAYS IN CASE OF ADJOURNED DEBATE
speechtext: In other words, why should the returned soldier in going to a doctor be put in a worse position in respect to medical treatment-which certainly the country owes him-than the ordinary individual? We are not doing this as a matter of charity; we are doing it as the recognition of an absolute right that the soldier has. I hope the minister will see that that rule disappears. It is a bad rule, it is a rule which is very one-sided and very unfair, working against the man who cannot help himself. There is another thing I think the minister would be well advised to do-to assure the House that such a case will not happen again. He tells that the case of Liddell has now been satisfactorily arranged. The minister sees how much pain and suffering has been caused in that case. I hope he will give us to understand something which at any rate I thought we would have all understood, that a man who was good enough and sane enough to be taken as a Canadian soldier, can never be deported. I think the minister will agree with me at once that in such a case it is an absolute negation of everything which we can look upon as right to say that the man who was good enough to fight for Canada ought under any circumstances to be deported.

subtopic: SUPPLY ON THURSDAYS OR FRIDAYS IN CASE OF ADJOURNED DEBATE

Mr. Chairman, may I be permitted to refer again to one or two cases, because you will understand that if they go over now they remain over for a year? The minister has in mind the Cornish case to which I referred. The doctor at Sydenham refused to operate, and the man was taken down to St. Anne's, where he was without any person with whom he could consult when the

operation was performed. I made it a point to visit the man and the facts are as I stated. The department sent a nurse to the man, but whatever good she could do by her report I do not know. I do not mean to say that the inspection by a nurse-

subtopic: SUPPLY ON THURSDAYS OR FRIDAYS IN CASE OF ADJOURNED DEBATE
speechtext: Could my hon. friend tell, me whether the toes were taken off both feet?

subtopic: SUPPLY ON THURSDAYS OR FRIDAYS IN CASE OF ADJOURNED DEBATE
speechtext:
I am replying now to a medical man. This soldier was taken to hospital for examination. He was operated on for varicose veins, and his condition was very much improved. When he was at Kingston the doctor refused to operate on his feet Later the man was removed to St. Anne's away from his people, and the doctors there thought they could improve the overlapping condition of both great toes by straightening them, but the operation was a failure; his toes are now rigid and he tumbles over when he attempts to walk. In fact he cannot even get out of his house. In the meantime the board got behind the technicality in the regulations which I think should be removed, and in this I think the minister will agree with me. The other point I desire to refer to is with regard to reports on file. The Liddell case was affected by such reports. But there are two other cases where the same thing occurred. One is the Duckett case. Let me repeat the circumstances. Duckett was a Scotchman and in 1913 and 1914 was working at a bakery. Then came a demand for help in the Glasgow naval yards. He went there and worked two years. Then came a demand for firemen on the convoys carrying Canadian soldiers overseas. He believed he could do better service by taking this more dangerous work. He worked as a fireman for two years, until a German torpedo blew up his boat. Then he decided he would quit firing and on his last trip to Canada he enlisted at Belleville. After a few weeks of training he had a slight hemorrhage, and upon examination was reported to be one hundred per cent unfit. How in the world he ever passed the doctors in the first place I do not know. He was given a pension. At the end of four years the board decided that they had made a mistake and withdrew his pension. There is the greatest amount of detail given in the file on that man's case-twice drunk in Mowat, disorderly and incorrigible, then taken out to the West, discontented, and so on. I admit the board has done a lot for Duckett in a way, but he has been treated most unfairly in other respects. For instance, take his discontent while in the West. He was there for seventeen months getting treatment

Supply-Re-establishment
for tuberculosis. His wife at Sydenham appealed to him to come home and take his treatment at Mowat. He made application and was refused. I have referred to the psychic effect on these patients while undergoing treatment. The appeal of his wife to come home, and the refusal of the authorities to allow him to go got on his nerves. He took his discharge and went home. Then it is entered in his file that he was very discontented! He was out there seventeen months, but there is nothing else against him. Yet the minister in his letter to me referred to the fact that there was this charge against the man of being discontented. What man would not be discontented who was refused permission to return home? We are told he was drunk once at Mowat. But why should these things be brought up when you want to treat such a man fairly? Away back in 1912 he had a gLand removed from the side of his neck. After that he was employed in a bake shop. I have here a certificate in reference to those two years of service showing not one sign of sickness. I have also a certificate of his health in the naval yards and his discharge from the boat after two years' service without any sign of ill health. He enlisted and two months after his service commenced he showed signs of tuberculosis. He gets a pension for four years, but it is cut off after he has started to build up a home. This is where I say there is an indication of a lack of soul, a lack of sympathy on the part of the department concerned. Then, there is a case similar to that mentioned by the hon. member for West Calgary (Mr. Shaw). In this case the man was mentally deficient. However, he enlisted and made a good soldier. He went over to England, where he was sick. Then there is some discussion as to his sickness; and he returns with a disability by which he is unable to take hold of anything with his right hand. On account of this mental deficiency at the beginning, he is said to be not entitled to anything at all. These are the cases which seem to indicate that there is a lack of co-ordination, a lack of sympathy, and it is not only on the part of the pension board; it is found also in the Department of Soldierfe Civil Re-establishment.
