speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, it already has been suggested that perhaps some of the money which is going into administration had better go for the benefit of the ex-service sick or disabled. We have had a number of cases cited this afternoon of exservice men whose treatment by the department was lacking somewhat in sympathy. It cannot be. that the administration is overworked, because if we subdivide the headquarters staff here we shall at once perceive that nothing is more nicely classified and subdivided-unless it be the United States tariff. With the reduction in the number of patients throughout the whole country and the closing of certain hospitals one would expect some appreciable reduction in the headquarters staff. I think the minister's figures show that there has been a reduction of about 60 or 70 in this large staff. If the committee will bear with me I will go into the subdivision of the

Supply-Re-establishment
headquarters staff as given in the Auditor General's report. Of course the last one we have is for 1923. I think after hon. members have listened to this subdivision they will come to the conclusion that the headquarters staff might very well stand some further reduction, the money thus saved being devoted to the benefit of sick veterans. The subdivisions to which I would direct the attention of the committee are as follows: There is an Accounts branch with 72 employees; an Administration branch with 8 employees; an Audit branch with 12 employees; a Central Registry branch with 138 employees; a Dental branch with 7 employees; an Engineering branch with 45 employees, amongst them a general superintendent, an assistant superintendent, a chief electrician, a matron-whatever she does-two utility messengers and draughtsmen; a Loans branch-a new branch *-with 7 employees; a Pay branch, pensions, with 33 employees; a Pay and Personal branch with 54 employees; a Pay imperial branch with 121 employees-there are apparently three subdivision pay branches; a Personal branch with 9 employees; a Purchasing branch with 14 employees; a Records branch

in addition to the central registry-with 81 employees; a Statistical branch, with 19 employees; a Stenographic branch with 57 employees; a Stores branch with 68 employees; a general division with 10 employees; a Training and Inspection branch with 17 employees; a Treatment branch with 60 employees-an increase of 7 over the year before; an Orthopaedic branch with 4 employees; a Dietetic branch with 3 employees; an insurance branch with 48 employees; a Messengers branch with 16 employees. There you have at least three pay branches. I am sure the committee would like the minister to explain the difference in the work of these various branches. Then again I would draw attention to another overlapping which appears to me in this Unit branch. If a man in the Ottawa branch takes sick he reports to the Unit branch, whereupon two doctors examine him. Then he goes up to the Pensions branch, whose doctors re-examine him. In addition to the nine medical officers of the Pensions branch here, we have two other doctors doing Unit branch work right in this city. This looks to me to be a clear case of overlapping. As we have found out to-day, most of the doctors in the Unit branches are senior to the doctors at headquarters, yet their reports in many cases are overridden by their juniors, and this is the cause of a great deal of trouble in the treatment which the men receive. It is only in the subdivision of the Administrative branch that one can see a great number of employees, and it would be very interesting if the minister would explain this apparent overlapping and overmanning, especially in the case of the three Pay branches. This is another matter I think the minister might very well consider with a view to preventing overlapping. In such cases as have been mentioned here this afternoon the money might very well go to the men rather than to administration.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
subtopic: SUPPLY ON THURSDAYS OR FRIDAYS IN CASE OF ADJOURNED DEBATE
speechtext:
I do not share my hon. friend's view that the service is not being reduced at headquarters. In ten months there has been a reduction of 78 employees; that must surely be considered as substantial. We reduce our medical staff very slowly, because though the number of patients in hospital decreases, the number of applications for treatment and for pensions does not decrease very much. Unless the department is to close its doors and permit no claims of any kind to be made, where a returned man finds that he is suffering from trouble, some disease, some pain, and contends that it is due to his service, there is no course left to the department but to have the man thoroughly examined, his file drawn., his documents verified and all the facts considered in order that justice may be done. That procedure has to be followed even though no pension is awarded or no treatment given, and even at that, as my hon. friend knows, we do not succeed in satisfying everbody. So I say we have substantially reduced the staff, although nothing would be more agreeable to me than to be in a position to say that we had reduced not by 2,000 but by 4,000. As the years go on the reductions in the staff will be slower. I have been convinced that while in some sections or branches the number of employees may be a little too large, generally speaking the depart-men is cot overstaffed. I had -that impression three years ago but I dared not raise my voice because I was not then fully conversant with the situation. At that time I was struck by a figure of, if I mistake not, about 8,000 employees in the department, while to-day we have 2,800. It was apparent to me that there were too many employees, for at that time we had only about 5,000 patients, and to-day we have 3,600-not a great difference. The reduction has been going on steadily at an average of from 18 to 22 a week. If you have a heart, and I know you have, you cannot go any faster without creating serious hardship among the men that you retire. Let us be content with the reduction of about 20 a week; that will bring the staff down to a very small figure within a year or two. A number of large branches in the department have been
Supply-Re-establishment

done away with and the heads of them retired, so that to-day, practically speaking, we have only two branches in the department, the administration and the medical departments.

subtopic: SUPPLY ON THURSDAYS OR FRIDAYS IN CASE OF ADJOURNED DEBATE
speechtext: Suppose an exservice man at Carleton Place is sick and wants to get treatment; will the minister outline the routine in order to show the committee how many hands that man passes through before final action is taken?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
subtopic: SUPPLY ON THURSDAYS OR FRIDAYS IN CASE OF ADJOURNED DEBATE
speechtext:
My hon. friend is an able
medical man; he knows that the first physician this ex-soldier meets may be a general practitioner. If a chest condition is detected, for instance, the man will have to be turned over to the chest specialist, or the doctor in the unit, for further examination. No decision can be given at this stage without an X-ray examination, and the case would be turned over to the X-ray specialist for that purpose.

subtopic: SUPPLY ON THURSDAYS OR FRIDAYS IN CASE OF ADJOURNED DEBATE
speechtext:
He must go to
the unit man first, then he is referred on.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
subtopic: SUPPLY ON THURSDAYS OR FRIDAYS IN CASE OF ADJOURNED DEBATE
speechtext:
He is still in the unit:
he will have to be X-rayed and his plates carefully read. If he shows signs of mental deficiency, the specialist in mental diseases will have to be called in. This information will all be part of his file, and then headquarters will decide whether or not he is entitled to treatment. It may be
9 p.m. found that he is not entitled to treatment, and all this work, which may have required I do not know how many hours from two or three men, will have been paid for by the country. That is why it is difficult to reduce as much as some people would think.

subtopic: SUPPLY ON THURSDAYS OR FRIDAYS IN CASE OF ADJOURNED DEBATE
speechtext:
I may be wrong,
but I think the routine is a little more elaborate than that. The man is examined; a report goes out from the unit to have a private physician at Carleton Place examine him. Then he turns up at the unit office here, and after being dealt with is referred to a specialist. You have a medical officer in charge of the unit; you have two medical officers there as examiners before the man goes out. Then he is passed in from the unit to headquarters and the matter is dealt with there; he may be examined by two or three more men, or he may be sent either to Toronto or to Montreal. My opinion is that where you have headquarters and the units so close together, you could save a good deal of that trouble by combining these medical offices.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
subtopic: SUPPLY ON THURSDAYS OR FRIDAYS IN CASE OF ADJOURNED DEBATE
speechtext: That is a suggestion that I think is worth considering.

subtopic: SUPPLY ON THURSDAYS OR FRIDAYS IN CASE OF ADJOURNED DEBATE
speechtext:
What is the cost per patient
per day in the Calgary unit, and is the rental of the building included in that cost?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
subtopic: SUPPLY ON THURSDAYS OR FRIDAYS IN CASE OF ADJOURNED DEBATE
speechtext:
At the Belcher hospital
in Calgary the cost per patient per day for the six months from April 1, to September 30, 1923, was $3.46. Those are the latest figures I have for that hospital. The number of patient days for the six months was 24,031.

subtopic: SUPPLY ON THURSDAYS OR FRIDAYS IN CASE OF ADJOURNED DEBATE
speechtext:
Does that include rental of
the building?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
subtopic: SUPPLY ON THURSDAYS OR FRIDAYS IN CASE OF ADJOURNED DEBATE
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: SUPPLY ON THURSDAYS OR FRIDAYS IN CASE OF ADJOURNED DEBATE
speechtext:
I thought that would be
charged to the Public Works department.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
subtopic: SUPPLY ON THURSDAYS OR FRIDAYS IN CASE OF ADJOURNED DEBATE
speechtext:
We include everything in
the cost, so I am informed.

subtopic: SUPPLY ON THURSDAYS OR FRIDAYS IN CASE OF ADJOURNED DEBATE
speechtext: Regarding the doctors in small places who are employed by the department at so much per case do they investigate any cases without the authority of the officials of the department? In a place like Sydney or Glace Bay, for instance?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
subtopic: SUPPLY ON THURSDAYS OR FRIDAYS IN CASE OF ADJOURNED DEBATE
speechtext:
They have authority to
make examinations when they think it is advisable to do so.

subtopic: SUPPLY ON THURSDAYS OR FRIDAYS IN CASE OF ADJOURNED DEBATE
speechtext:
I think that would be
proper. I do not know whether it is part of their duty or not, but I am afraid that some of these doctors, after making examinations, do not always bring the cases to the attention of the department. I think they should take steps to bring cases that should be treated to the attention of the pension officer at Halifax or of the D.S.C.R. officials at Halifax or Ottawa. Everything possible should be done to find out whether these cases are in need of hospital treatment and to assist the patients in every way in getting such treatment. They should be brought to the attention of the pension officer or the department's officials. I had under my observation a year ago three cases in the city of Sydney, which a doctor was attending, I presume, on the authority of the D.S.C.R. headquarters at Halifax. He was a good medical man, but he did nothing to bring to the attention of the D.S.C.R. or of the pensions officials that these people required treatment. I happened to be in the city at the time, and two of these men sent for me. One of them was in a very serious state with tuberculosis. I took his case up with Mr. McPhee in Halifax and in less than thirty days the man was in Kentville sanatorium, and the result is that he is now very much improved. I would think that these

Supply-Re-establishment
doctors when they attend a case, should take steps to find out whether or not the man is suffering from a disability requiring hospital treatment, and if so, the doctor should do his best to have him brought into hospital. I am not finding fault with any particular doctor or doctors, but I am just bringing this matter to the attention of the minister because two of these cases came under my own observation, and I believe that if this man had not been given treatment in Kentville sanatorium he would have been dead by now, but as it is he is making very fine progress. I think it should be part of the doctor's duty to do everything possible to get hospital treatment for the men needing it.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
subtopic: SUPPLY ON THURSDAYS OR FRIDAYS IN CASE OF ADJOURNED DEBATE
speechtext: That is their duty..

subtopic: SUPPLY ON THURSDAYS OR FRIDAYS IN CASE OF ADJOURNED DEBATE
speechtext: The minister said there was a reduction in the staff of about twenty per week. Can this rate be maintained indefinitely without seriously affecting the efficiency of the service to the patients? speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
subtopic: SUPPLY ON THURSDAYS OR FRIDAYS IN CASE OF ADJOURNED DEBATE
speechtext:
I have already expressed
the opinion, Mr. Chairman, that it will not be possible to reduce at that rate very much longer. We shall have to slow down somewhat. As to what figure should be considered the minimum for the staff to be, that is a pretty big contract -to place in my hands. I would think probably five hundred in, say, three years. After that, when most of the patients are in the homes, and when the period has elapsed during which men can apply for treatment or pension, that figure will be considerably decreased, but we shall require quite a large clerical staff to pay pensions. A number of pensioners are not permanent. They receive a pension that will undoubtedly be decreased, suspended, or cancelled entirely within one or two or three years. These cases require periodical examinations. I am unable to say at the present time exactly at what day the minimum will be reached, or what that minimum will be.

speechtext:

minister give us some information about the insurance scheme for soldiers which comes under this item. How many men are insured, and what is the amount paid? I think the committee would be interested in hearing the details.

subtopic: SUPPLY ON THURSDAYS OR FRIDAYS IN CASE OF ADJOURNED DEBATE
speechtext:
What is the percentage
of deaths among those who hold policies?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
subtopic: SUPPLY ON THURSDAYS OR FRIDAYS IN CASE OF ADJOURNED DEBATE
speechtext: I have not the percentage n my mind at the moment, but I know it is luite satisfactory, considering the fact that these men have been accepted for insurance without any medical examination, and in the majority of cases it is only reasonable to assume that it is the men who were sick or suffering from some disability who have sought insurance rather than the men who were well.

subtopic: SUPPLY ON THURSDAYS OR FRIDAYS IN CASE OF ADJOURNED DEBATE
speechtext:
Are there no figures
to indicate the percentage?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
subtopic: SUPPLY ON THURSDAYS OR FRIDAYS IN CASE OF ADJOURNED DEBATE
speechtext:
I could find the figures if
I had a little time. I do not remember them at the present time, and I dare not make an estimate.

subtopic: SUPPLY ON THURSDAYS OR FRIDAYS IN CASE OF ADJOURNED DEBATE
speechtext:
Is the reduction of over
$500,000 for hospital treatment due to a reduction in the number of patients?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
subtopic: SUPPLY ON THURSDAYS OR FRIDAYS IN CASE OF ADJOURNED DEBATE
speechtext: That has to be -taken into consideration, but it is reductions in staff mainly.

subtopic: SUPPLY ON THURSDAYS OR FRIDAYS IN CASE OF ADJOURNED DEBATE
speechtext:
With regard to insurance,
I kpow, of course, that these men have been accepted without medical examination, and that naturally the prospects would not be as good as those of an ordinary life insurance company. But could the minister give us an estimate as to what percentage of loss is to be expected? What percentage will the government have to put up to carry this scheme along? speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
subtopic: SUPPLY ON THURSDAYS OR FRIDAYS IN CASE OF ADJOURNED DEBATE
speechtext: It is difficult to estimate what the loss will be. Undoubtedly the loss to the country will be large. I have seen an estimate of about $20,000,000.

subtopic: SUPPLY ON THURSDAYS OR FRIDAYS IN CASE OF ADJOURNED DEBATE
speechtext: Over what period?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
subtopic: SUPPLY ON THURSDAYS OR FRIDAYS IN CASE OF ADJOURNED DEBATE
speechtext:
Over the whole period, because no other man can avail himself of insurance now the new 1-aw is in effect. The mortality rate under the Returned Soldiers' Insurance Act is not exceptional considering , the class of risk which is taken. During the current year 299 claims were received by the department. Of these 65 were settled under section 10, and so on.
Supply-Re-establishment

subtopic: SUPPLY ON THURSDAYS OR FRIDAYS IN CASE OF ADJOURNED DEBATE
speechtext: Has the minister the figures of the ordinary insurance company in proportion to that number of claims?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
subtopic: SUPPLY ON THURSDAYS OR FRIDAYS IN CASE OF ADJOURNED DEBATE

subtopic: SUPPLY ON THURSDAYS OR FRIDAYS IN CASE OF ADJOURNED DEBATE
speechtext:

subtopic: SUPPLY ON THURSDAYS OR FRIDAYS IN CASE OF ADJOURNED DEBATE

speechtext:
May I ask what
the difference is between item 293 "Care of patients and medical examination of pensioners" and the item "Hospitals and clinics"? They are both large votes and the second amounts to $2,000,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
subtopic: SUPPLY ON THURSDAYS OR FRIDAYS IN CASE OF ADJOURNED DEBATE

subtopic: SUPPLY ON THURSDAYS OR FRIDAYS IN CASE OF ADJOURNED DEBATE
speechtext:
With regard to the staff
employed at Ottawa I have before me a return brought down by the department. With respect to that organization in the department known as the purchasing and stores division, I find that in 1920 there were 221 employees engaged in purchasing to the amount of $3,001,088.51. In 1921 there were 259 employees and the amount of the purchasing was $2,062,916.31. In 1922 the number of employees was reduced to 172, and their total purchases amounted during that 
year to $1,229,796.29. In 1923 the number of employees had been cut down to 110, and their total purchases for that year amounted to $1,117,135.20, a diminution in personnel of 62 and in purchasing of $112,000. Then in the year 1924, according to this statement the staff was further diminished to 92 and the amount of purchases during that year totalled $836,368.50. It does not seem to me that the reductions in staff have in any sense been proportionate to the amount of the purchases actually made, and it would appear that here is a very likely source from which the minister could secure a substantial reduction in the staff. I also have the salary paid these officials and I find that during last year there has only been a decrease of something like $20,000 in salaries. I would suggest to the minister that in this purchasing and stores division there should be an opportunity to dispense with the services of a considerable number of men. If that is not possible the minister might co-ordinate the purchasing division of this department with that of some other department and perhaps eliminate practically all of the staff.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
subtopic: SUPPLY ON THURSDAYS OR FRIDAYS IN CASE OF ADJOURNED DEBATE
speechtext: I think there is something in the remarks made by my hon. friend. I may say that I have followed pretty closely the reduction of the staff, but in all these matters the minister has to rely mainly upon the advice of the chief officials. It may be that in this particular instance the reduction has not been proportionate to the amount of purchases made. I will look into the matter more carefully and see if there is a possibility of making a further reduction.

subtopic: SUPPLY ON THURSDAYS OR FRIDAYS IN CASE OF ADJOURNED DEBATE
speechtext: I point out the fact that there are three pay divisions at headquarters. Will the minister kindly explain what these are?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
subtopic: SUPPLY ON THURSDAYS OR FRIDAYS IN CASE OF ADJOURNED DEBATE
speechtext:
I did not catch my hon.
friend's question?

subtopic: SUPPLY ON THURSDAYS OR FRIDAYS IN CASE OF ADJOURNED DEBATE
speechtext:
There is a Pay
branch, pensions, 33 employees; Pay and Personal service, 54 employees; Personal division, 9 employees; and the Pay, imperial branch division, 21 employees. I have taken these figures out of the Auditor General's report, 1923.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
subtopic: SUPPLY ON THURSDAYS OR FRIDAYS IN CASE OF ADJOURNED DEBATE
speechtext:
The Imperial Pay branch
is under the Administrative branch and it is entirely supported by the Imperial government. Still we have to do the work; we have to provide the staff, and the pay of the employees but this expenditure, of course, is refunded to the department. There are only, as I said a minute ago, two main divisions-

Supply-Re-establishment
the administrative and the medical. All these branches my hon. friend refers to will come under the Administrative branch. The Pay and Personal branch, like the Purchasing and Stores division-in fact all these divisions- had a head and stood by themselves some three or four years ago, but they have now been contracted although they bear the same names and are under the one administrative head.

subtopic: SUPPLY ON THURSDAYS OR FRIDAYS IN CASE OF ADJOURNED DEBATE
speechtext: Still there are three sub-division pay branches. The amount paid out by the Imperial branch is given here as $7,000,000 requiring 121 employees; whereas our branch paid $50,000,000 and has, I think, only 33 employees. And then there is the Pay and Personal branch for our own service.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
subtopic: SUPPLY ON THURSDAYS OR FRIDAYS IN CASE OF ADJOURNED DEBATE
speechtext: That is quite right.

subtopic: SUPPLY ON THURSDAYS OR FRIDAYS IN CASE OF ADJOURNED DEBATE
speechtext:
And this branch
will have 54 employees for a total staff of something like 2,000.

subtopic: SUPPLY ON THURSDAYS OR FRIDAYS IN CASE OF ADJOURNED DEBATE
speechtext:
Could there not be a
combining of these different pay branches into one pay department?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
subtopic: SUPPLY ON THURSDAYS OR FRIDAYS IN CASE OF ADJOURNED DEBATE
speechtext:

in charge of it now.

subtopic: SUPPLY ON THURSDAYS OR FRIDAYS IN CASE OF ADJOURNED DEBATE
speechtext: Is there any reason why there should be 121 employees paying out $7,000,000 in British pensions and 33 employees paying out $50,000,000 in Canadian pensions?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
subtopic: SUPPLY ON THURSDAYS OR FRIDAYS IN CASE OF ADJOURNED DEBATE
speechtext:
My hon. friend is aware
that the Imperial section is not merely a paying division. It deals with provisions for examination of Imperial pensioners, of expensioners in Canada requiring treatment, and I have always considered that the staff of the Imperial section as certainly not too large. I am surprised my hon. friend says that it is large, because it is one branch where I think it is pretty hard to effect a reduction. We have been very careful not to overload the Imperial government with a staff which is not needed. I assure my hon. friend that there is a great deal of work to do in the Imperial section.

subtopic: SUPPLY ON THURSDAYS OR FRIDAYS IN CASE OF ADJOURNED DEBATE
speechtext: Is there any comparison between the work done by the Imperial section and that done by the Canadian section?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
subtopic: SUPPLY ON THURSDAYS OR FRIDAYS IN CASE OF ADJOURNED DEBATE
speechtext: In some regards there is.

subtopic: SUPPLY ON THURSDAYS OR FRIDAYS IN CASE OF ADJOURNED DEBATE
speechtext:
In the Canadian
section there are 33 employees paying out $50,000,000 and handling the cases connected with that, and in the Imperial section ^there are 121 employees paying out only $7,000,-
000 and handling the cases in connection with that. It looks as if the number of employees in the Imperial section was large.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
subtopic: SUPPLY ON THURSDAYS OR FRIDAYS IN CASE OF ADJOURNED DEBATE
speechtext:
There is quite a large
number of Imperial pensioners in America. The Imperial section has to deal with Imperial pensioners in both Canada and the United States. There are in all 18,000 Imperial pensioners in America.

subtopic: SUPPLY ON THURSDAYS OR FRIDAYS IN CASE OF ADJOURNED DEBATE
speechtext:
But still the
$7,000,000 amount covers them all.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
subtopic: SUPPLY ON THURSDAYS OR FRIDAYS IN CASE OF ADJOURNED DEBATE
speechtext: Yes.

We shall not have very

to medical men?

Treatment allowances.

I am afraid I shall have
to ask the permission of the committee to ask one or two questions on the last item, because I understood this covered pay to medical men. speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
subtopic: SUPPLY ON THURSDAYS OR FRIDAYS IN CASE OF ADJOURNED DEBATE
speechtext:
I do not think that out
of the few hundred medical men on the strength of the department, more than three or four have been changed.

subtopic: SUPPLY ON THURSDAYS OR FRIDAYS IN CASE OF ADJOURNED DEBATE
speechtext:
In the case of the three
or four who have been changed, will the minister explain-not individually-on what ground the changes have been made?

subtopic: SUPPLY ON THURSDAYS OR FRIDAYS IN CASE OF ADJOURNED DEBATE

In one case the man
resigned because he was dissatisfied with the department. That is the unit medical director at Montreal, who made a protest against the
Supply-Re-establishment

department placing a layman at the head of Ste. Anne de Bellevue hospital. We discussed that question this afternoon. I think his brother resigned from Ste. Anne de Bellevue hospital and we had to replace him. We changed the unit medical director at Halifax some few years ago. I do not think besides those we have changed a single medical director in Canada.

subtopic: SUPPLY ON THURSDAYS OR FRIDAYS IN CASE OF ADJOURNED DEBATE
speechtext:
Not a medical director,
but there was a change made in the medical officer at the head of the lakes at Port Arthur.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
subtopic: SUPPLY ON THURSDAYS OR FRIDAYS IN CASE OF ADJOURNED DEBATE
speechtext: That may be.

subtopic: SUPPLY ON THURSDAYS OR FRIDAYS IN CASE OF ADJOURNED DEBATE
speechtext:
I need not mention the
name. The minister can easily look it up. There was an officer who had come back from the front and who had several years' service overseas. He had served as medical officer at the head of the lakes for some years. He became president of the Conservative Association, and shortly afterwards he was practically dismissed, asked for his resignation, and a Liberal put in his place who had not been overseas. I point this out because I think it is a very unfair proposition. I can see no other grounds for this being done than politics. The man who had this done to him wrote to the director, Dr. Mclvor, and he replied that he was instructed to make a change. I presume the instructions came from Ottawa I asked about the other changes because I did not know whether any had been made or not. I put questions on the order paper in regard to this matter, and I have been unable to ^ find any cause for his dismissal, because it is practically that, except politics. speechtext:
I would like to put on record now some matters in connection with the work of the Federal Appeal Board so that the minister may. have an opportunity of dealing with them when the item is taken up. I have received numerous petitions of various kinds, and I wish to read from, a couple of them so that when the time comes the minister can deal with them. One is from the War Veterans' Association at Calgary. I will read the material part of the letter:
Veterans in Calgary are dissatisfied with the manner in which these cases are heard, in particular the fact that the appeals are heard before one member of the board only, and judgment is reserved in all cases. We would respectfully suggest that the travelling board consist of three members of the board who would hear all cases and announce decision in the name of the board instead of a quorum of the Appeal Board at Ottawa again sitting on each case before decision is arrived at. We are of the opinion that this would be a means of saving to the government. Allowance of appeals by the Board of Pension Commissioners and D.S.C.R. after appellant has been heard is also unsatisfactory. These departments have already had their opportunity when examining the pensioner or appellant prior to appeal. Appeals from pensioners or appellants should be final in so much that if upheld by Appeal Board action should be taken to rectify injustice done to appellant and if adverse decision, decision would be final also and we are of the opinion

Supply-Re-establishment
more satisfactory to all concerned. Appellants should be given benefits of doubts as to originality of disability within reason, which is not done at present. We would also suggest that appeals against reduction of pensions should also be within the scope of the Board of Appeal. The entire powers of the Appeal Board could be greatly widened to the benefit of all concerned and undoubtedly cost less in the long run to have these matters adjusted.
A long series of resolutions was passed at a largely attended public meeting of the citizens of Weyburn, Saskatchewan. I will read those which have reference to the work of the appeal tribunal:
1.	That the time for appealing to the pension Appeal Board from the decisions and rulings of the Pension Board be extended.
2.	That the scope and jurisdiction of the pension Appeal Board be enlarged so as to include assessment for disability in cases where the pension or allowance is complained of as being insufficient and the ruling of the Pension Board in that respect unfair and unjust.
3.	That the pensions be increased to the extent of the present bonus.
4.	That whereas the pension Appeal Board as at
present constituted cannot reasonably and does not efficiently and speedily dispose of the work for which it was created.
And whereas the present system of dealing with appeals is cumbersome and unduly expensive, and is largely ineffective and leads to undue and unreasonable delay in dealing with the cases of disabled soldiers and the widows and orphans of soldiere who met their death in the performance of their duty to Canada and the Empire, and who during these long delays are without the means of sustaining life and must in the meantime depend upon the charity of their old comrades and of their sympathetic fellow citizens in the several communities in which they reside;
And whereas it has now been fully demonstrated that no single appeal tribunal can possibly hear and dispose of the very large number of appeal cases throughout the Dominion under the most favourable conditions, there being in Saskatchewan alone oyer 600 cases awaiting appeal, and even if it could that the unavoidable long delays would be the cause of great suffering which should at all cost be avoided.
And whereas if these appeals are to be efficiently and promptly dealt with,
Now it is resolved that some other system and method of appeal should be adopted.
It is further resolved and urged that the ruling or judgment of the Court of Appeal be final and binding upon the Pension Board and that the continuance of its present disregard and defiance of the law of Canada, as enacted by the people's representatives in parliament, be visited upon the members of the Pension Board by the most severe penalties, as in the case where ordinary citizens commit a breach of any of the more vitally important laws of the country.
A further resolution goes on to deal with some rather drastic punishments which it is suggested should be meted out to the pension board and also the officials bf the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment. I simply want to bring these recommendations, which are typical of many I have received, to the attention of the minister, so that when the matter comes up again he will probably be able to advise us as to his suggestions in regard to improving this appeal procedure.

subtopic: SUPPLY ON THURSDAYS OR FRIDAYS IN CASE OF ADJOURNED DEBATE
speechtext:
There is one case I have particularly in mind. The minister will possibly remember that I took it up with him by correspondence. It seems to me that in that case the man has been very unfairly treated, and by reason of this case and other

Supply-Re-establishment
cases of a somewhat similar nature, a general impression has been created that the medical boards of the department are anxious to keep down, so far as possible, the amount of the pensions. It has even been suggested that instructions have been given to the medical men to keep down the pensions, and to disallow pensions wherever that is possible. I am quite sure that no such instructions were issued by the minister, but the impression does prevail that, either directly or indirectly, instructions to that effect have been given. If that is a fact, I think it is a most discreditable thing, and I am forced to the conclusion that there must be some foundation for it, because in my opinion the medical boards are not treating these men with any degree of fairness. More than that, if statements made to me are correct, they are telling one story to the men and are making different reports to the department. That has been repeated to me time after time, and I say that kind of thing should be stopped. It is absolutely wrong; it is inhuman. I feel there is certainly room for some improvement in the method of handling the cases which come before the medical boards, and that there is not that degree of sympathy that should be shown to the men who have served their country like these men have done.
The particular case to which I refer, it seems to me, is a typical one. I have given the minister the particulars. I could give the man's name now, but I presume nothing would be gained by that, but if it is desired, I shall do so. It is the case of a man who served overseas and was very badly wounded. He had a gunshot wound in the head. He has quite a hole in his forehead; it is very noticeable; indeed it is so large you could almost put your thumb in it. He has another wound on his lip, which causes it to look like a hair-lip. He had an operation, and a piece of shrapnel was taken out of his head; there is another piece of shrapnel still in his head. That man has a wife and family, and is receiving a pension of, I think, $39 altogether. He is in very bad shape; he is a physical and nervous wreck. So far as I am aware no other cause has been assigned for his condition than his war services. There is nothing in his record which would give the faintest indication of any other reason. The man is certainly not in a fit condition to work. He is subject to fits of an. epileptic nature which occur very frequently and he is unable to sam a livelihood. When I took the matter up with the minister I received a letter from his secretary stating that the case would be reviewed, and in the meantime the man would 170

be taken on the strength in Vancouver. I sent a copy of the letter to the man and in due course he got in touch with the department in Vancouver for the purpose of being taken on the strength where, I presumed, he would come under observation and his case be satisfactorily dealt with. However, he ascer-
' tained from the officer in charge of the medical service in Vancouver, Dr. Proctor, that no instructions had been received from Ottawa to that effect. Dr. Proctor was of the opinion that the man was not qualified to be taken on the strength because he was physically capable of working. Apparently that was not the opinion of other government departments because when this man applied for various positions with the Department of Customs and the Department of Immigration on the border in my constituency he was informed that owing to his disabilities his application could not be considered at all.
After taking the matter up with Dr. Proctor I was informed that some arrangement was going to be made to take care of this man and in due course learned from the man what that arrangement was. It appeared that if he could make an arrangement with some employer who would guarantee that at the end of two months he would give him permanent employment the department would pay his wages in the meantime. That is to say, the department would pay the wages for two months but at the end of that time the employer would have to provide a permanent position. That seemed to me to be absurd. I thought the man must be mistaken and I said to him "Have you anything in writing to that effect?" He said: "No, but I think they would give me a letter to that effect", and I have that letter. Now, here is a man who is not able to work. Yet they tell him that if he can find some employer who will guarantee to employ him permanently at the end of two months the department will pay his wages in the meantime. I can read that letter to the committee if any doubt is entertained in the matter. It seems to me there is something wrong with a system under which such a proposition as that can be made. The trouble with the man is that he is not able to work. But what I am objecting to is that the board in Vancouver takes the objection that the disability if there is disability is not due to war services at all, or at least that that fact has not been established, that the onus of proof is on the man himself. Surely such an attitude as that is ridiculous. As a matter of fact, the man has been aided by an organization of a more or less charitable character
Supply-Re-establishment

at the coast. Through its agency the man was sent to Chicago where one of the most eminent surgeons on the continent is located with whom he got in touch. That surgeon happened to be the very one who performed the first operation on the man in question. I have statements signed by that surgeon testifying to the man's condition, accompanied by X-ray photographs showing clearly that there is still a piece of shrapnel in his head. And yet according to the opinion of the medical advisers of the department something more than that must be proved. Surely such an argument as that is most inhuman. I cannot imagine how the minister, after hearing all these facts, could allow the matter to rest as it is. In my opinion quite a different attitude should be adopted. Here is a man who should be getting a fair and reasonable pension, because if I am any judge at all he is a physical and nervous wreck, and his condition is undoubtedly due to his war service. That is one case.
I have another case where a man had lost one eye and is getting a pension of $7.50 a month. What do you think of that? It is unbelievable but it is a fact. And that pension of $7.50 was only granted after a great deal of effort. The man is not satisfied with it, of course. He does not consider the pension a fair one; neither do I. That man served overseas and his eye was injured. Upon returning to Canada he went to the department and after keeping him under observation for some time it was decided that the eye must be taken out. It was removed and a glass eye substituted for it, and now the country pays him the magnificent sum of $7.50 a month. The reason assigned for not granting him a larger pension was that his eye was not in a good state when he went overseas. It is true that some fourteen years previously one of his eyes had been injured, but he still had the use of it and was in such good physical condition that he was accepted for service overseas. And to-day he is in receipt of the generous pension of $7.50. There is something wrong when it is possible for such treatment as this to be meted out to men who have given good service to the country.
I could go on and give further instances of unfair treatment, but I shall not do so because the chairman of the special committee investigating the cases of returned soldiers has stated that in all probability I shall have an opportunity of bringing the facts in my possession before the committee. However, I might relate the case of a man who served overseas with the Seventh battalion, was wounded there, is now in very bad shape but is not receiving a pension. Why? For two
IMr. McQuarrie.]
reasons; first, because he was over age when he enlisted. I have no sympathy whatever with an argument of that kind. They were not objecting that he was over age when the country required men. They were not objecting that he was over age when they sent him to the trenches, and he was right in the hottest part of the fight. He was wounded there. He was sent to England by instructions of General Odlam who was his officer commanding at the time. He went into hospital in England, and after he got out of hospital he was placed in "C" category. He might have come back to Canada at that time, but he said:	"If I can do any work here of a
clerical nature, I will stay, and I will let some man who is fit go overseas." He did that. Now they say to him: You should not have enlisted in the first place; that is where your trouble comes in, and in the second place, you were a very short time in the service and you had a good job in England. It is a terrible indictment of somebody when such things can happen. If they say that this man was a short time in France, what would they say about the glorious dead who were a much shorter time in the field than he was? If the Board of Appeal has any merit whatever, its jurisdiction should be increased so as to cover cases like this. As it is, these men have no place to go with their complaints except to the medical officers, who, as far as I can see, are anxious as much as possible to keep down expenditure, to keep down pensions, and to keep men from getting pensions wherever possible. I suggest that the minister 'who is, I believe, doing his very best to accord fair treatment in deserving cases, should take under advisement this question of increasing the jurisdiction of the appeal board, or of having some kind of tribunal where men who are getting inadequate pensions can go and be assured of receiving a fair and square hearing.
